about/index.html.body: Skip to content ☰ Home Coached by Tom Female Performance Plan Only Plan Store About Us Blog Contact About Us The coach behind Horsepower I'm Tom Cooling, Founder and Head Coach at Horsepower Coaching, and I bring a rare blend of lived experience and academic expertise. An ex-elite triathlete, seasoned ultra-bike racer and FKT holder, with a first-class degree and a master's in sport science behind everything I coach. Tom Cooling, founder and head coach of Horsepower Coaching Coaching experience I've spent over a decade coaching athletes from complete beginners to world-tour level professionals, guiding competitors to wins and podiums across Ironman, middle-distance triathlon, ultra-bike events and Haute Route-style races. Where it comes from It comes from my own racing, including FKT performances and ultra wins, from training alongside Royal Marines and UKSF, and from coaching elite performers. I know first-hand what the hard days actually take, and that goes into how I build and read every athlete's training. Philosophy I combine the evidence-based methods professional athletes rely on with practical, race-proven strategy, with a particular emphasis on female-specific performance development and durable, race-winning preparation. It's quality over quantity, and a no nonsense, holistic approach: one good block was never the point. What matters is a whole athlete, ready to hold up on the day it counts. National Time Trial Championships Qualifications The credentials behind the coaching Sport science First Class BA and Master's Degree in Sport Science and Athlete Development. Breathwork and freediving Oxygen Advantage Advanced Breathwork Instructor, and AIDA L4 Freediver. Core Temp Accredited Coach Heat and climate adaptation, from designing the protocol to executing it on race day. XTRI Extreme Triathlon Accredited Coach Accredited for the extreme end of the sport, the XTRI races like Norseman and Celtman. Mountain leadership BMC (British Mountaineering Council) Trained and Assessed Mountain Leader. Tom on the start line Racing it, not just coaching it The coaching is grounded in racing. Ironman and 70.3 podiums, Haute Route weeks in the Alps and the Dolomites, the Lost Dot TransPyrenees: the same kind of preparation Horsepower athletes get, tested first-hand. blog/f/2017-season-wrapup---calm-after-t.body: Skip to content ☰ Home Coached by Tom Female Performance Plan Only Plan Store About Us Blog Contact Blog / 25 January 2021 2017 Season Wrapup - Calm After The Storm By Tom Cooling · 25 January 2021 Bar a few cross country runs, my triathlon season is all but over. I'm staring down the barrel of a much needed break from structured training and 4 months in Indonesia and South Easy Asia. I'm buzzing about the adventure, being able to sea swim every day and taking a break from the accumulated mental fatigue from what has been a very testing year. Looking forward to swapping this... For this! Despite showing a lot of promise at the beginning of the 2017 season, two lacklustre performances have left me with a dirty great chip on my shoulder. When I began writing this post the coin was still flipping midair between heads - dropping down to half iron distance and enjoying the sport or tails - dusting myself off and climbing back in the ring for another round with a fearsome adversary.... I've since stumped up the cash and signed up for one more round with this fire breathing, claw toting, indomitable welsh dragon. I've only ever done Ironman Wales as a last minute entry not knowing what to do at the end of triathlon season but this time it will be my main focus. This will be my fourth Ironman triathlon and my third bash at Wales so I know what's coming. I just need to learn from the lessons this season saw fit to teach me and turn up a different, better athlete. Taking a 4 month gap from training initially worried me but now I think it may actually do me the world of good. A clean break from what I've been doing up until now and a chance to start a complete fresh and focus on technique in the meantime. 50 Weeks To Get Lei'd I know if I'm going to stand a chance at jumping into my finest flowery shirt, getting Lei'd and being given the opportunity to empty my bank account into the Ironman coffers for a coveted ticket to Kona I will need to be faster than a greased weasel.... So how am I going to do it??? Phase 1 - Off Season Rebuild In my four month break from the miserable UK weather I'm going to be stranded on this island for 10 weeks; Not only is this place surrounded by some of the last remaining coral reefs that humans haven't managed to f*ck up yet, its miles from anywhere, and its conveniently shaped like a running track... A sandy 1100m running track to be exact. The plan is to focus on rebuilding my running technique and lose my sloppy loafing style and hit next season a high cadence machine. The clear protected waters inside the reef will be perfect for swimming so I can continue to work on my swim technique without being lunched by any predatory fish. Other than the swimming and running I'll be putting some quality time into flexibility and core work. Two things that I have definitely neglected up until now. Phase 2 - Easy Does It! When I return from playing Robinson Crusoe we're going to be moving to what I've dubbed as the triathlon mecca of the South West... No its not Boulder, Colorado... its Clevedon! Complete with a marine lake perfect for open water swimming, some great running routes, cycling hills in close proximity and a beautiful 15 mile ride into Bristol. After analysing the hell out of my training from this year with my new Training Peaks Platinum account I've realised one thing; I tried to model myself as triathlon's version of Emil Zápotek who was famous for the high load HIGH intensity training approach. This did one thing.... cooked me by the time I got to July and left me feeling flat not to mention constantly knackered and unable to walk up stairs. The most telling piece of information from my Training Peaks analysis session was this; My 5 minute power to weight ratio (watts/kg) was on the cusp of domestic pro standards and 20 minute wasn't too shabby either. My ability dropped off as the efforts got longer as shown by my 60 minutes watts/kg falling into the Cat 2 region. This confirmed that my training has made me great at big short distance efforts but I can't sustain it. I've been reading quite a lot lately on the 80/20 technique where 80% of your training load is easy (Z2) and 20% is a mix of moderate (Z3) and hard (Z4). I feel like this might be the key to helping me manage a higher training load and improve my ability to sustain a high output for longer. Matt Fitzgerald's book 80/20 running provides a good insight into the technique. If you are going to have a go at adopting the 80/20 approach its definitely worth going out for a run or ride and without looking at your Garmin, go at a pace that you think is easy. Then take a look at the end of the session and see if it actually was. My easy lunch run today was well into the moderate heart rate zone and definitely emphasised the points made in the 80/20 article and Matt Fitzgerald's book about people spending too much time in zone 3 when they think they're running easily. So, with the 80/20 regime in mind I've devised the following hours based program; 8-10 hours a week bike commuting - Easy 3-4 hours bike on the indoor trainer - Hard 4 hours running - 3 Easy & 1 Hard 2-3 hours swimming - 2 Easy & 1 Hard Totalling 17 - 21 hours a week depending on the period of training, 80% of which will be easy Z2 work leaving me with a few hours to go hammer and tongs. In another effort to make my bike training specific to my goals I have changed my existing fixed gear track bike commuter for an cheap TT bike that mimics my race bike position and allow me to log some serious training miles in the TT position, hopefully reducing the gap between my road bike FTP and TT bike FTP figure. Phase 3 - RaceHard! Racing is awesome fun.... but its expensive and can sometimes derail your big A race plan if you struggle to recover and re-peak in time for the main event; something I suffered from in 2017. The plan is, keep it specific but break it down into events where I can truly measure my ability in each discipline; open water swims, 25, 50 and 100 mile cycling time trials and running races including some off road runs and half/ full distance marathons. Some of these events will be turned into bricks by combining a run off the bike after a time trial or maybe cycling to a run event. Get help! I need it! I'm just trying to suss out of which variety and how much help I need. Do I go fully coached or steer my own ship??? Answers on a postcard! Historically I've found I don't play well with others and like the control of writing my program. I don't need any extra motivation, I'm more than happy burying myself on a daily basis... I just need another pair of eyes to look at me and the program and tell me if I'm doing too much or not enough. 2018 targets; Get my 1,000m swim TT below 14 minutes and 4,000m below 60 mins. Get my one hour bike power back above 325w (67-68kg body weight) Go sub 55 minutes for a 25 mile TT. Break 2 Hours for a 50 mile TT. Get my running back in order starting with a sub 2:50 target time at the Newport marathon in April. Improve my average run cadence to 180spm across the board. And last but not least; Tear the Ironman Wales course apart next September! Now for some much needed chill time and to put together the build spec of my sexy new race bike for 2018.... ← Back to the blog Train with Horsepower If that is how you like your coaching, straight and built for your race, take a look at the training plans or see how coaching works . blog/f/dont-get-fancy-before-youre-fancy.body: Skip to content ☰ Home Coached by Tom Female Performance Plan Only Plan Store About Us Blog Contact Blog / 7 August 2026 Don't Get Fancy Before You're Fancy By Tom Cooling · 7 August 2026 Most athletes reach for the fancy stuff long before they've earned it. New wheels, a heat protocol, ketones, some exotic interval format off the internet, all while their easy days are a mess and they've not done a single session that looks like their actual race. So here's the blunt version I give my athletes: don't get fancy before you're fancy. Nail the basics first, because that's where nearly all of your improvement is sitting, unclaimed. What is the low-hanging fruit? It's the boring stuff that works. For almost everyone reading this, the biggest gains are still sitting in three places, and none of them cost a penny. Consistency. The single most powerful thing in endurance training is turning up, week after week, without the big gaps and the boom-bust cycles. Twelve consistent weeks beats four brilliant weeks and eight lost ones every single time. If your training history has holes in it, that's your first and biggest gain, and no gadget touches it. Specificity. Your training should look like your event. If you're racing a hilly long-course triathlon, your key sessions should rehearse hills, duration and race intensity, not generic blocks that could belong to anyone. Train the demands you're actually going to face. Your biggest limiter. Everyone has one thing holding them back more than the rest. Fix that first. Spending your effort polishing a strength while your limiter sits there untouched is the most common way I see people train hard and improve slowly. Get those three right and you'll beat the athlete with the better kit and the worse habits nearly every time. Why do the basics get ignored? Because they're not exciting, and because the fancy stuff is where the marketing lives. Nobody sells you consistency. There's no product for turning up. The industry makes its money on the one per cent gains, so the one per cent gains are what fill your feed, and it's easy to convince yourself the reason you're not improving is a missing supplement or a smarter interval structure, rather than the eight weeks you took off over winter. There's an ego cost to the basics too. Riding genuinely easy on your easy days feels like you're not trying. Doing the same specific race-simulation session again feels less clever than inventing a new one. Facing your biggest limiter means spending your training time on the thing you're worst at, in front of everyone, which is uncomfortable. All of that pushes people towards the shiny, complicated work and away from the plain work that actually moves the needle. Honestly, a big part of my job is just giving people permission to keep doing the boring thing that's working. How do I find my biggest limiter? Look at where the race actually falls apart for you, not where it feels hardest in the moment. If you fade badly in the last third of every event, your limiter is probably durability or fuelling, not top-end power. If you get shelled on the first steep climb, it might be your VO2 ceiling. If your easy pace and your race pace are almost the same number, your aerobic base is thin and that's the whole job. Be honest here, because the limiter is usually the thing you least enjoy training. That's precisely why it stayed a limiter. The other honest test is to look at your training, not your intentions. Pull up the last couple of months and ask what you actually did, not what the plan said. If ninety per cent of your rides look the same, medium-hard, medium-length, no real easy and no real hard, then variety and structure are your limiter before anything physiological. If you never once trained the specific demand of your event, specificity is your limiter. The data usually tells you plainly what you've been avoiding. What does specificity actually look like? Specificity isn't a slogan, it's a set of concrete choices. Take a hilly long-course triathlon as the example. Specific training means your long ride isn't a flat aerobic cruise the whole way through; in the final third it carries the climbs and the race-effort blocks you'll actually meet on the day, held at the intensity you intend to race, with the fuelling you intend to use. It means your long run rehearses running on tired legs, at the pace and duration the race demands, not a comfortable trot on fresh ones. It means your key bike session confirms the wattage you can genuinely hold for the real duration, so your race plan is built on numbers you've actually produced rather than hoped for. Generic training builds generic fitness. It's not that a random hard ride does nothing; it's that it does less, per hour, than the same hour spent rehearsing the thing you're trying to be good at. The closer your training looks to your event, the more of your fitness shows up on race day instead of staying in the gym. When am I allowed the fancy stuff? When the basics are genuinely handled, not when you've decided you're bored of them. The advanced work and the marginal gains are real, but they're marginal by definition. A one per cent gain from some clever intervention is worth chasing once you've already banked the twenty per cent sitting in consistency, specificity and your limiter. Chase it before that and you're decorating a house with no foundations. There's an order to it, and the order isn't negotiable: Show up consistently for long enough to build a base. Make your key sessions specific to your event. Find your biggest limiter and put real work into it. Only then start layering in the refinements that turn good into slightly better. The short version You don't need the fancy stuff until you've earned it, and most people haven't. The unglamorous work, turning up, training the actual demands of your race, and hammering your weakest link, is where the improvement lives. Do that properly for a season and you'll be amazed how far it takes you before you need a single marginal gain. Get fancy after you're fancy, not before. ← Back to the blog Train with Horsepower If that is how you like your coaching, straight and built for your race, take a look at the training plans or see how coaching works . blog/f/everesting---climbing-the-mountai.body: Skip to content ☰ Home Coached by Tom Female Performance Plan Only Plan Store About Us Blog Contact Blog / 25 January 2021 Everesting - Climbing The Mountain By Tom Cooling · 25 January 2021 Late one evening I got a text from a good mate... it read "do you fancy Everesting with me next year?"... Without really understanding what Everesting was I immediately replied "yeh sure thing". A quick google search later and the enormity of the challenge really sunk in... To set the scene I'll jump back two years before Mike sent me this text... I'd just found out some pretty earth shattering news...my Granddad had cancer. Not really knowing how to help I signed up for an event called Tumble Up 4 Life (https://tumbleup4life.wordpress.com/) to try and raise some money for charity. This involved doing hill repeats on the infamous 'Tumble' climb (Abergavenny, South Wales) to raise money for Cancer Research UK. The Tumble is no easy climb, it features in the top 100 cycling climbs list and rightly so; the 2.8 mile segment averages 8% as it kicks up 1295ft. The climb is a morale breaker; the first part is steep with two tight bends, the road straightens and continues to climb to the well known cattle grid that marks roughly half way. As the trees give way to open mountain top landscape the wind picks up and batter you as you churn away to the summit. I used the TumbleUp4Life as a reason to start riding my bike more seriously. Prior to that I used to go out and do maybe 30 or 50 miles and think that was enough but now I had a motivation to push. With the company of a good friend, Stuie Morris, I made the 20 mile cycle from my home in Monmouth to the Tumble to make my preparations. This started as climbing it twice, then three times, then one day I managed 5 times. Its funny how having such a strong motivator makes poor weather and fatigue seem insignificant. The day of Tumble Up 4 Life arrived and with a fully stocked car and an eager support crew I set about trying to summit the mountain 10 times. The first climb went without incident but on the turn around at the bottom I slipped and stupidly put my hand out... with a sore wrist (turned out to be a cracked Scaphoid) I pushed on. Fatigue was mounting and the wrist growing increasingly more painful as the climbs ticked by. After climb number 8 I knew that was enough. I was absolutely gutted not to complete my pledged 10 climbs but I still managed to raise nearly £1000 for Cancer Research UK. Fast forward back to the text from Mike... My google search had confirmed what we needed to do.... we needed to climb the height of Mount Everest... on our bikes... in one ride... in under 24 hours... just let that sink in. I enthusiastically tapped away at the screen on my phone and Mike got the following reply "WHAT?! you want us to climb 29,028ft in one ride? Mentalist! I'm in!" The idea behind this event wasn't just about pushing ourselves; I had unfinished business with this climb after failing to make my 10 ascents two years before and Mike had the recently found out the sad news that his Nan had cancer. This is why cycling is so special, especially a Sisyphean task such as hill repeats; It can be a means of letting you process grief, anger or sadness. As a rule, I've never finished a ride feeling worse than when I started it. It really saddened me to hear that Mike's nan passed away last week. I'm so glad we got to do something like this Everesting that can be forever in our memory dedicated to her. The 29th April 2017 came around, the day of our big push for the summit. Mike and I met at the foot of the climb at 5am ready to summit the beast 23 times. We had already raised over £1000 for Cancer research UK and with dawn approaching we kicked off. After the noise and fanfare of racing Ironman this was such a weird day. Weird in that there is nobody shouting and cheering (well apart from our ultra loyal support crew!), there are no competitors to race...there is just silence and the constant thrum of your bike gears spinning over as you climb. I knew from Ironman that we had to take it slowly, any big efforts early on would be paid for 10 fold later in the day. Mike and I climbed at different speeds just because we were different sizes etc. We ended reaching a constant rhythm of passing each other as one climbed the other was descending. YES!! 10 climbs banked! I had buried my previous challenge but was still not even half way. We had 23 climbs to do to make the height gain of Everest! I was lucky enough to have a visit from a good mate who agreed to pace me up a few of the climbs just to keep my rhythm going. Rhys' visit couldn't have been better timed as I went through a bit of a low spot between climbs 10 and 13 and he kept my pace up. One thing I remember was eating SO much... Brioche with peanut butter, banana and strawberry jam as my snack of choice with pizza and chocolate as backup. This was all washed down with a curry that I pretty much fell asleep into at the end of the ride. Strava said I burnt a shade over 9000 calories so I think it was allowed. The climbs ticked by as the legs grew heavier. Finally made it to climb 20! It was getting cold by this point so I took 5 minutes in the car to warm up. As Mike finished his 20th climb I jumped out of the car full of beans shouting "only 3 more to go!!!!"... he rolled over and showed me his Garmin, it showed he only needed 2 more climbs to make the Everest height gain! I couldn't believe it! Mine showed I needed 3! It was getting dark and I didn't really want to be finishing alone! Luckily at a weight light enough for a stiff breeze to have me (68.5kgs) I climb fairly well. I set out and buried myself on the next two climbs. I managed to catch up with Mike who was half way up his final climb and we managed to reach the summit together. Thank God that's over!!! Once my ride was uploaded to Strava and the HELLS500 website (www.everesting.cc/hall-of-fame/) I found out that I'd set a new fastest time for Everesting this climb. Needless to say, I was pretty damn happy with that! A few bits of advice for anyone who fancies a go... Be Light Climbing on a bike is just simple physics... #P2W The lighter you are the less energy you have to produce to lift the weight up the hill. With this in mind don't turn up on deep section wheels with a heavy bike, a heavy toolkit, or litres of water. If you're supported you should really only take what you need to complete the climbs and leave your extra food, water and main toolkit in the car. Stop every few climbs for a resupply. Pacing Everesting is a marathon not a sprint. I found the Everesting Calculator (http://everesting.io) website really helpful to suss out how long it was going to take based on my climbing wattage and weight etc. This took the guess work out of how fast or slow I needed to go. Keep your effort level even and don't go too big or into the red. Keep to your target climb times even if you feel great. That feeling will pass. Nutrition You are going to be on the bike for probably 15+ hours. You need to keep eating. I always go for a little bit often and try to alternate from sugary stuff to savory to avoid getting an upset stomach from sugar overload. Also being outside constantly getting hot on the climbs and cold on the descents takes it out of you. Try and get a warm drink or meal into you if you can. Mindset This is a long, slow and tiring endeavour. No matter how fit or strong you are, or even how many Ironman races you've done, the fact you're repeatedly climbing the same bit of road over and over again will cause your mind to wander. Loss of concentration can lead to negative thoughts and its something you need to expect. Finding a reason that goes a bit deeper than just wanting to be awesome helps a lot. Raise money for charity, dedicate the climbs to someone so you feel like you can't quit on them. I always find it helpful to break each climb down into sections and trick myself with a food reward at the top. Basic puppy training right there. [Get in touch if you have any more questions about Everesting or how to prepare. ]() ← Back to the blog Train with Horsepower If that is how you like your coaching, straight and built for your race, take a look at the training plans or see how coaching works . blog/f/female-first-not-female-adapted/i.body: Skip to content ☰ Home Coached by Tom Female Performance Plan Only Plan Store About Us Blog Contact Blog / 12 August 2026 Female First, Not Female Adapted By Tom Cooling · 12 August 2026 Most training plans are built for a man and then shrunk. Fewer hours, lighter weights, softer targets, same physiology underneath. That's female-adapted, and it's lazy coaching. I do it the other way round. The female athlete is the default, not the exception, and that decision runs through everything from how the plan is built to how I read the sessions that come back. What does "female-first" actually mean? It means the plan is designed for a female body from the first line, rather than a male template with the numbers turned down. Menstrual cycle, hormonal context, symptom load, life load, the lot, treated as things that matter, not a disclaimer at the bottom of the page. I coach a small roster of women who race at the front, and they're the proof I trust more than any brochure. Hannah S won Ironman Wales in 2022. Madison S won it in 2025. Naomi S and Elly B have podiums and wins across some of the hardest races going. I keep the full list of what these women have done on my female performance page , and every line of it comes straight off their race results. Those are results, not marketing, and the coaching behind them is female-first because the athletes are. Should women train around their menstrual cycle? This is where a lot of the noise in the sport overclaims, so I want to be honest about what the evidence supports and what it doesn't. The headline claim you see everywhere, "train hard in the follicular phase, back off in the luteal phase," isn't well supported. The largest synthesis we've got, the McNulty et al. 2020 meta-analysis, found that the effect of menstrual cycle phase on exercise performance is small, and on average close to trivial. More importantly, the response is highly individual. Some women are genuinely flattened in the days before their period; others notice almost nothing; a few feel strongest at points a rigid model would tell them to rest. So a plan that hard-codes "smash the follicular phase" is selling a certainty the science doesn't have. If the average effect is small and the individual variation is large, then the coaching answer isn't a fixed prescription. It's to track the individual. So what's the actual win? Two things, and neither of them is phase-prescription. Symptom management. The performance shift across the cycle may be small, but the symptoms are real and they're what actually derails sessions: cramps, heavy bleeding, sleep disruption, migraine, gut trouble, the flat low-motivation days. Coaching that helps an athlete plan her quality work around her own symptom pattern, adjust fuelling and hydration, and stop treating a bad-symptom day as a fitness failure, is worth far more than a colour-coded phase chart. Closing the education gap. Surveys of female athletes repeatedly find that a large majority, roughly seven in ten, report their cycle affects their training, yet under a third have ever been given any education on how to work with it. That gap is the real problem. The voices worth reading here are the honest ones: Emma Ross and the well+ team, Georgie Bruinvels, Kirsty Elliott-Sale. They don't oversell. They teach women to understand their own response and make decisions from it, which is exactly the job. How I actually coach it Cycle-aware, not cycle-deterministic. If an athlete wants to log her cycle and her symptoms, that becomes one input among several, alongside sleep, life stress, how the last block has gone and what we're trying to build, that I use to decide whether today's a day to push or a day to protect. I don't lock a woman out of a hard session because a chart thinks she's in the "wrong" phase. I look at what her body is actually telling us, put it in context, and explain the call I've made. Athlete-trusted, coach-led. What does female-first change beyond the cycle? The cycle gets the headlines, but treating the female athlete as the default changes a lot of quieter decisions too. Fuelling is one. Under-fuelling is common in endurance sport and the consequences are more serious for women, because chronic low energy availability disrupts hormonal function and bone health in ways a male template will never flag. A female-first plan treats adequate fuelling as non-negotiable, and it doesn't quietly reward the under-eating that a lot of the sport still celebrates. Strength work is another. It's not a bolt-on for women, it's central, for bone density, for durability, for injury resistance and for raw performance, and a female-first plan protects it rather than dropping it the moment the schedule gets tight. And life load matters. Many of the women I coach are balancing training with careers and caring responsibilities that don't pause for a training block, so the plan has to bend around real weeks without treating a missed session as a moral failure. None of that's exotic. It's just what coaching looks like when the female athlete is who you designed for from the start. Is female-first only for elite women? No. The palmares is the sharp end, the proof the method holds up against the best fields going. But the same principles, honest cycle-awareness, proper fuelling, protected strength work, a plan that bends around a real life, matter just as much for the woman training for her first sportive or her first half-distance triathlon. Arguably they matter more there, because she's the one least likely to have ever been coached this way. The short version Female-first is a design decision, not a marketing line. The cycle matters, but it matters through symptoms and individual response, not through a rigid "train hard now, rest now" rule the evidence can't back. Track the individual, manage the symptoms, close the education gap, and coach the woman in front of me. That's the whole method, and if you want to see how it plays out, it's all on the female performance page . ← Back to the blog Train with Horsepower If that is how you like your coaching, straight and built for your race, take a look at the training plans or see how coaching works . blog/f/how-not-to-coach---the-art-of-lis.body: Skip to content ☰ Home Coached by Tom Female Performance Plan Only Plan Store About Us Blog Contact Blog / 25 January 2021 How Not to Coach - The Art of Listening By Tom Cooling · 25 January 2021 Listening is a wonderful thing. If you do it right you can learn things, become aware of opportunities, avoid problems... the list goes on. Last year, in an effort to achieve my peak peak potential, I decided I might have to stop listening to myself and pay a coach to get me there. I submitted to the plan and 'the process' (a triathlon phrase that has become synonymous with the lengthy pursuit of physical improvement) and went about 'getting it done' (another triathlon phrase that is often used in a self-congratulatory manner to emphasise the completion of a potentially mundane/boring training session in the face of great adversity). This post was inspired by my good friend Lawrence Cronk and his honest account of being quick, but not rapid . It will be a brief journey through my 2018 season, the impact of not listening to myself or being listened to and what happens when the machine you spent years building, falls apart... AND so its not all negative and downhill, the story of the biggest come-back story since Rocky 3. 2018 Season So 2018 was to be my second year of seriously trying to do well in long distance triathlon. As all of you will know, holding down a full time job, a relationship, and the training schedule required to be able to race an Ironman, is no easy task. I agreed with my partner Jo, if I was going to do it all over again then I would do it properly. I knew that I had the power on the bike and the speed on the run but I needed endurance, a lot more endurance. I needed to be more hammer and less scythe, so sought out the best coach in the business. After some exciting chats about what might be possible I began ticking off the sessions set for me. As the sessions kept coming and coming and I kept going and going, there was no doubt over the fact I was getting fitter and faster. The other thing that was apparent was growing tired and increasingly more bored. I was unwilling to admit that I was struggling... Not listening to myself perhaps? Training because less of a joyful escape but more of a chore. Although I've never been the social butterfly, I watched my diary slim down to nothing more than key birthdays and my Training Peaks itinerary. I kept telling myself I had to see this through...It will all be worth it on the Ironman Wales finish line i'd say. Cracks started to appear a few months. I'd put together 2-3 weeks of good training, show signs of improved numbers on the bike and run but would then end up with a cold or a mouth full of ulcers and spend the following week where I should have been enjoying recovery, laid up feeling like crap. This cycle continued until I got to my DIY training camp in August, still a month away from the race that I just wanted over and done with. I put together 3 days of good quality sessions before I hit the wall, a mental wall. I remember banging my head against the the living room wall, bib shorts in hand just thinking I can't get back on the bike, I was way too burnt out to go for a run and there was no way I could face staring at the black line at the bottom of the pool. I was saturated with boredom and needed a break. The allure of achieving my dream sub 10 hour finish time at Ironman Wales seemed completely pointless. From that day on I stopped getting motivated by seeing a full sweep of activities completed on Training Peaks and I started missing days. If the growing number of missed/ incomplete sessions and repeated bouts of illness weren't enough of a message, the concerned messages about feeling battered and needing a break should have been. But was it listened to? More unplanned recovery days and incomplete sessions started to creep in as my body and mind took turns in deciding which couldn't take it. When the body was playing ball, I could perform at a level I only dreamed of before... but the sad fact of it was, I didn't really care. Ironman Wales So the big day rolled around. The excitement I felt the previous 3 times I've toed the finish line were non-existent. There were no nerves, no worries, just this numbness. Race morning arrived and still numbness. I put on a bit of Elder Island, set up my bike in transition and made my way down to the beach. Photos with the family and a good bye and good luck from everyone. No tears were shed when the 10,000 people sang the Welsh National Anthem on the North Beach of Tenby, I just looked around, followed the group and dived into the murky water. Swim banked in 62 minutes. The endless hours doing drills in the pool seemed to have paid off. Out onto the bike, not before dropping it and losing a bottle of nutrition in the process. This was to be the mistake which defined the day... Freshwater West bound and the power felt good as I moved up to 26th overall. The endless hours riding to race power had made this kind of output feel easy. As I passed Tenby the first time, despite riding an even flat power (1.02vi) on the hilly course, the lost nutrition bottle which I failed to stop and replace caught up with me. I bonked my way from miles 85-100 before stopping at the top of the climb in New Hedges. After inhaling what felt like 20 energy bars, pieces of dried mango, coconut cake and a coffee (kindly provided by one of the amazing Ironman volunteers) I headed off into Tenby. My heart was low as I descended, I could see the time on my bike computer showing 6 hrs 55 minutes elapsed. I had a bit of a reflective 5 minutes. I questioned what it was all about, what I was chasing and why I was here. Yes, I dreamed of the sub 10 but I knew to achieve that I was going to need to run 3:00 flat on the marathon; a time I was more than capable of. I started wondering what that would prove, what Ironman was all about and what it would mean to me when I finished. As I racked my bike I considered how much I was willing to hurt myself to achieve that run time. The answer that came back was one I had already asked 3 weeks prior to Ironman Wales. On my final big training weekend before the taper I ran what I can only describe as a crazy run session; 2hrs 30mins duration made up of half marathon pace work then marathon pace with repeated surges to 10k pace for the remainder. This pushed me to the point of collapse and I promised myself I was done. I ran around Tenby on a victory lap. Not a victory because I'd done especially well in the race but because I'd finally remembered to listen to myself and trust my instincts. Jo was cheering from the side of the road cheering me on shouting out time splits to the leaders of my Age Group. I just replied "I can't wait to finish, I'm done" as I continued jogging around... I wasn't prepared to give any more of myself to it. I crossed the line in 10hrs 34mins 18seconds with a smile on my face and a sense of peace. The Big Crash In the weeks that followed the race I felt crap. I hadn't achieved the dream sub 10. I hadn't even come in the top 10 of my age group. I wasn't annoyed or disappointed because I didn't have a flash time to band around, I was disappointed because I knew that I wasn't hungry on the race day. I think I could have hit my desired finish time if I'd been 10-20% less fit but 50% more hungry for it. I was deeply over-trained and run down by the time the race came around. In retrospect, something I feel was obvious had the signals been listened to. Four weeks post race I started feeling dizzy and a constant niggling headache. I had zero energy and couldn't walk up the stairs without reaching for the handrail. This carried on for a few weeks until I was sat in work and the right side of my face dropped. Sat there petrified because I couldnt feel my cheek I had the harsh reality that I might be having a stroke hit me. After numerous trips to the doctors and the neurology department I was told that I'd had a mini-stroke and was suffering from an inner ear virus that was giving me constant vertigo. After nearly 3 months off work with endless days stuck on the sofa, the dizziness stopped. I started to feel more normal and less like I'd never ride my bike again. At the lowest point I couldn't walk up a set of stairs without needing to take a break so the prospect of going on a long ride felt a million miles away. The reason I've chosen this picture for the blog is because like Sisyphus, the man who became famous for deceiving the Greek Gods to cheat death and invariably ended up with a worse punishment, I too failed to see when it was my time to stop... I too ended up with a worse punishment as I learned about over-training and not listening to myself the hard way. ← Back to the blog Train with Horsepower If that is how you like your coaching, straight and built for your race, take a look at the training plans or see how coaching works . blog/f/how-to-improve-your-triathlon-swi.body: Skip to content ☰ Home Coached by Tom Female Performance Plan Only Plan Store About Us Blog Contact Blog / 2 February 2021 How to Improve Your Triathlon Swim By Tom Cooling · 2 February 2021 The Black Magic of Swimming I think its fair to say, unless you swam competitively as a child, really getting to grips with swimming quickly can feel like black magic. How many of you reading have felt that sinking feeling of your feet being tickled half way down a 25m length as the swimmer behind threatens to overtake? You respond by trying to swim harder and harder to get away only to surface at the end of a swimming pool lane flustered, breathless and feeling like the water temperature has increased to that of a hot bath. The questions that follow usually go along the lines of: "I'm fit so why can't I swim faster", "I'm sure my catch was right???", "was I kicking enough?", "how are they so fast and not beetroot red???" Its a complete drag hey? Well this this blog is an insight into my slightly different approach to swim training for triathletes. Something that if you can get your head around, it will change the way you see the water and hopefully set you on a course to faster more efficient swimming. Water Ok so its easy to feel like water is triathlete enemy number one. Well to quote Sun Tzu "if you know the enemy and know yourself, you need not fear the results of a hundred battles". The reason I'm quoting The Art of War is knowing your enemy, water in this case is the key to overcoming it. There is a bit about knowing yourself (i.e. what you're doing in the water) but we will come onto that later. So, water is everywhere, we're made of it, we need it to survive... we need to swim through it to get through a triathlon etc etc etc. The main thing you need to remember that unlike riding your bike through air that breaks relatively easily, water is circa 800 times more dense than air (depending if we're talking salt water or fresh) . Everyone is constantly bombarded with aero this and aero that when it comes to reducing drag to cycle faster... but the principle is SO much more important when it comes to your swim. Drag There are several forces at work as you try to swim, some you are in control of and others not. For the purposes of this we're going to work on the assumption that you're floating ( yes your legs might sink - covered later ) but you're at the top of the water column and not stuck on the bottom of the pool. So the two we're interested in are thrust force (your kick and pull) and the drag force (how hydrodynamic (read: slippery) you are). This is the key...different things moving through the water experience different drag coefficients: a rough brick would experience more drag than a smooth sphere for example or a human wearing baggy shorts would experience more drag than one wearing swim trunks. Even if you don the most slippery swimsuit on the market, you're still going to need to use 80% of your energy just to get through the wet stuff. Ever walked across the shallow end of a pool? How hard does that feel? The amount of drag you experience, in a similar way to cycling aerodynamics is down to frontal area - viewed head on, the amount of you trying to break a path through the water. Minimising this frontal area is fundamental to improving your swim efficiency. The way I explain this to my coached athletes is to imagine they are a bullet punching through a piece of paper (the paper being the water). The size of the bullet hole created in the paper is usually dictated by the size of their hips and shoulders because you cant make them smaller. The idea is to make everything else (arms, legs and head) fit through that hole. Now if you imagine every time you're moving through the water you need to fit everything through that hole to maintain your minimum frontal area, when your legs and hips sink a bit you need to break a bit more paper and create a bigger hole, that's more drag... maybe as much as 20-40% more drag. Relating this back to Newton's 3rd Law (for every action, there is an equal and opposite reaction), your legs dropping increases your frontal area which means unless you apply more forward force on the water to maintain the same speed, you will slow down. This slowing down is significant. Some drag hydrodynamic drag coefficient equations suggest that at a steady state swim speed, every 1% of increased drag results in a 0.34% decrease in speed. So those legs dropping a bit and increasing your bullet hole by 20% just slowed you down by 6.8%. In a real world example, say you swim the Ironman swim leg in 1 hour 5 minutes on your best day, that increased drag would add 4 minutes to your swim split. That is unless you start working harder and burn some matches early on - not the ideal start to a long day out. It doesn't sound much but age groups and podiums are won and lost by smaller margins. What Can You Do? So now you know a bit more about your enemy and forces that are out of your control. Lets move on to things that are within your control. This may sound simple but this 5 point list I think is the starter pack for efficient swimming. 1 - Tension Tension Tension This is a bit of a simple one you can do at home.... Stand on your tip toes with your arms above your head. Try and be as tall as you can and reach the the ceiling. Remember what that body tension feels like, your pointed feet, tight and controlled core, long and thin shoulders, pointed fingers... That's what you need to carry into the pool to keep your body long and thin and make sure you're fitting through that hole neatly. 2 - Exhale Yes I know you haven't taken a stroke yet, but you need to learn this before you start because it is one of the biggest barriers to people being able to enjoy and relax into their swimming. As a rule, if you try and exhale and inhale when you turn your head to breathe you will quickly develop an oxygen debt because unless your head is on the side for an age, there isn't enough time to swim properly and do both the exhale and inhale in the same rotation. If your face is in the water, you're gently exhaling the entire time! Not only does this mean when you rotate to breathe, you only need to breathe in so you can relax about it because you have enough time... but it also means that you don't have a chest cavity jam packed full of air... air that floats and causes your legs to sink. 3 - Streamlined & Know It That sounds obvious but its the first step in the process. What we're looking for is for you to develop an appreciation of what streamlined feels like so you can identify when you're doing it wrong. The key for this is channelling that tip toe body tension you practiced in point one into the pool. You want to be pushing off the wall and gliding as far as you can without kicking or moving into a full stroke. Feel the water moving across your back and shoulders, focus on how that changes when you're gliding through it quickly and when you eventually slow down. Keep practicing that trying to glide further and further and further. The key isn't pushing of the wall harder, its about making your body as slippery and as long as possible. 4 - Hips Don't Lie Ever felt like your hands and feet aren't connected when you're swimming? The key is your hips. So you have body tension and a good streamlined position that cuts through the water and you've paid attention to what that feels like. Now you need to introduce rotation. It doesn't start from the hands or feet, it starts from the hips. Try the torpedo drill but as you glide along the surface of the water drive a steady rotation from your left to your right from your hips. Keep doing this until you feel controlled in the rotation and can feel the water breaking on your sides as you move. Feeling the water breaking here is an indication your hips are high enough in the water column and passing through the bullet hole your shoulders created. Don't forget the tension, don't forget the bullet hole. To quote Frosty from Chasing Mavericks... "steady rhythm, drive and glide" 5 - Kickety Kick Now we need to introduce your feet into the equation. Building on your rotating torpedo, you can add a little rhythmic kick. This needs to be driven again from the hips, doesn't need to be especially forceful, its main purpose is to keep your legs and hips elevated in the water. If you lose that little bit of foot propulsion your legs will drop and you're right back to the bullet hole drag problem. Point your toes, keep your body long and tense, rotate from the hips and keep kicking. You should feel the water breaking over the back of your toes. Keep checking back through points 1-4... Can you still notice the water moving along your back when you're gliding quickly? Can you still feel the water breaking on your hips when you rotate? Keep practicing and keep feeling. 6 - Inhale Up until now you've just been doing extended glides and breathing out... now its time to introduce breathing in. Some people prefer to inhale on one side, some on both. The argument for inhaling on both sides is it fosters an even and balanced stroke and can aid in swimming in a straight line and can help with open water swimming navigation. The best way of doing this is when you're doing your torpedo rotation drill with the little kick we covered in point, when you rotate onto your right (with your left hip high) twist only your head a bit more to the left enabling you to take a breath (your lungs should already be empty if you read point 2 so this should be easy). Try and breathe in every three rotations so you end up with a nice balanced bilateral breathing rhythm. *Check Yourself* - Its not a bad time to work back through the points you have already covered. At this point we haven't added the biggest disruptor to your hydrodynamic drag so providing you can kick, rotate and breathe without impacting on your streamlined shape, you're doing well. A good way of checking this is you should be covering much more distance now you're kicking than at the start. It should also feel pretty relaxed and easy. You should be able to feel the water and might be enjoying the experience. 7 - Arms, Elbows & Polar Bears Ok now hopefully you have a long, slender, tense torpedo like body and have mastered rotating from the hips while you're gliding (and exhaling) and now you can also breathe bilaterally. Now you need to introduce your arms into it. This is the bit that usually messes up that perfect streamline. If you remember your kick is responsible for keeping your legs afloat and promoting a good position in the water, your arms are the thing that actually propel you forward. Going back to the forces acting upon the swimmer, the arms are responsible for the thrust force. People who aren't efficient swimmers usually start by trying to work on their catch and pull in an effort to make them faster when really its the last piece of the puzzle. You make yourself as slippery as possible first, then you add propulsion. That way, your precious energy isn't being wasted unduly fighting the water. There are two points to an effective propulsive arm movement: Wide Arms - One of the biggest issues swimmers suffer from is hand crossover by swimming with too narrow a hand entry. This absolutely robs you of propulsive power because it stops you recruiting your lats to drive you forward. The red line is your centre line, this is your axis of rotation and a line you must not let your hands cross. If you exaggerate swimming with a slightly wider than you think you need hand entry, you will probably come out with the perfect entry (obviously don't go too crazy). Moving your hand along its yellow line is its most efficient path to generating force. High Elbows - Now this is commonly confused with the shape of your arm on the recovery part of your freestlye stroke (the bit that happens when your arm moves back from your side to the front of your stroke). Within reason, what happens above the water is pretty immaterial. You might have a beautiful looking stroke above the water but that wont make you fast through it. What high elbow actually refers to is what's happening at the front of your stroke. You need to concentrate on when your hand enters the water (wider than your shoulder) that your hand cuts deep into the water, that will naturally drive it lower in the water column as your momentum pushes you over your arm. If you don't observe the high wrist, high elbow rule you will end up overgliding and your fingers will glide up to the surface. When you do this you're effectively giving the water a big high 5.... something which is tantamount to a handbrake. The last element that is important to the propulsive part of your swim stroke is you actually pushing the water behind you to drive you forwards. One of the best means of improving this is practicing using the doggy paddle or polar bear swim drill. When doing this drill you don worry about the recovery phase, your hands stay in the water all the time. You purely focus on rolling from the hips, driving your hands forwards and down catching the water pulling you forward. This may seem like a lack of emphasis on propulsion but usually, when you sort out someone's rotation and position in the water, the catch and propulsive phase of their stroke fall into place. Hot Tip - Swimming is full of stuff you can buy that professes to be a magic bullet that will cure issues in your stroke. I'll save you a bit of time (and money) and let you know there are really only two bits of kit you need... neither are especially expensive and both are hugely supportive in developing an efficient stroke. Finis Axis Pull Buoy - Now this isn't any pull buoy (no this isn't a sponsored plug), its actually a genuinely great bit of kit that completely supports the hip drive freestyle stroke. You could effectively recreate it with a pull buoy between your calfs and a rubber band but I've used this extensively and can totally vouch for its effectiveness. Tempo Trainer - I'll cover more on this in the last point. 8 - Cadence Now this is the fine tuning of the stroke you have developed in the previous points. You have a full and efficient freestyle stroke if you've followed the previous points and its time to look at how quickly you do it. To do this you will need a tempo trainer. Finis do a quality one that you fit to your goggles and it uses a metronome to guide your turnover. Again this isnt a sponsored plug, its purely a great product I would genuinely recommend. Swim cadence is a funny thing, you can increase arm turnover and your speed will increase as a result because you're pulling the water more frequently. This increase in speed will carry on to a point when your perceived exertion increases and stroke quality drops significantly. There are several drills you can do, 10 x 100m for example where you start with the cadence you have naturally arrived at, and you increase it by 2 or so strokes per minute each interval recording your perceived exertion and time for each. There will be a sweet spot where you stop getting faster (the point your stroke quality has degraded). The ideal cadence for you is the fastest speed before your perceived exertion ramps up. Conclusion Thankyou for reading, I appreciate its a long blog post but swimming is complex. The main purpose of this was to explain you probably don't need to get stronger or start messing around with swim bands or even swimming particularly fast that often, you just need to focus on getting slippery in the water and making your bullet hole as small as possible. Then and only then can you look at propulsion and the rate at which you propel yourself to really fine tune your stroke. [If you have any questions about any of the skills, drills or this whole logical approach to swimming then feel free to get in touch. ]() Dedication Pretty early on in my swim journey I turned up at the University of Bristol swimming pool and met a guy who shaped my understanding of swimming. This guy, this legend in speedos is Alan Wood, the head of Wood Trained Swimmers. Sadly Alan, passed away at the back end of 2020. The words in my blog aren't his, they are my logical take on how to swim faster but he needs mentioning because not only was he a friend, he inspired me to look further into swimming faster and supported me as an athlete in the pool. Its fair to say the way he coached swimming had a massive impact on the way I coach and approach athlete development. It truly was an honour to have shared a lane with him! ← Back to the blog Train with Horsepower If that is how you like your coaching, straight and built for your race, take a look at the training plans or see how coaching works . blog/f/into-the-unknown/index.html.body: Skip to content ☰ Home Coached by Tom Female Performance Plan Only Plan Store About Us Blog Contact Blog / 2 February 2021 First Ironman - Into The Unknown By Tom Cooling · 2 February 2021 So after years of putting it off I finally got a job that paid enough for me to justify blowing what felt like a fortune on a race entry, my ticket to Ironman Nice 2016 was booked. I was 29 and with 30 rapidly approaching I knew I needed to man up and get this done or the regret of leaving the Royal Marines would continue to burden me. I had absolutely no idea of what this all involved, how it would feel, what I needed to do. My most recent multi-sport event was over 5 years ago and was a fair bit shorter (Super Sprint). Still, I had 12 months to get myself in some kind of iron worthy shape and answer all of these questions I had. One of the big misconceptions of Ironman training is the volume required to complete one. Any google search will leave you thinking that you need to be up at 4am daily and put in around 20 hours a week with endless long slow miles on the bike. I'll happily tell you that you can get around an Ironman with a lot less than 20 hours a week, it might just be more painful... The first 4 months of training were ok at best. At the time I was struggling with the combined pressure of a difficult job and caring for my Grandfather who was in the latter stages of cancer... I switched my drive to work for the bike which gave me around 150 miles a week of cycling and bolstered this with the odd evening run, spin class when my legs could take more bike time and the odd swim. Suffering at spin class It went on like this for a while, I knew I wasn't putting my all into it but it still seemed so far away... I wasn't swimming a great deal because I knew my technique wasn't the best and I didn't really like feeling bad at something, I wasn't running much because I was already a decent runner and I didn't want to ride more on the weekend because I'd spent the whole week on the bike... see the picture... excuses excuses excuses. The highs and lows of bike commuting The weather turned sour over the winter and I met Jo and training took a bit of a dive. I knew I needed to do something to get this Iron show on the road so I started playing to my strengths... I started running; hilly and fast... the kind I loved but not the kind that would get me around an Ironman marathon. I finally stopped flogging myself up hills and swapped to running 3 half marathons a week at a pace I thought I could hold together for a marathon off the bike. Despite being happy running through rain and snow in the bitter depths of winter, I still couldn't bring myself to go out on the bike unless it was nice. I hadn't been swimming in months either so I knew I would have to survive most of the course and rely on my strong run to get me home. A good example of a typical non-ironman training run As the race drew closer I knew I needed to do something to sort myself out so I booked a weeks leave from work and did my own training camp at home in the Wye Valley. I named this 'Cheeky Week', after a week in Marines training that serves as a thrashing to get you to the next tier of fitness. That week was a bit of a milestone for me; I managed to conquer my first solo hilly century ride, suss out a vague nutrition plan and nearly caught hypothermia after bullying myself to go swimming in the river. I came out of the week feeling slightly more prepared. Trying to find some form on the bike during 'Cheeky Week' 2 weeks out from the race I dropped the training load and attempted a taper. Although I hadn't trained a lot each week, I had definitely become used to the constant trickle of endurance exercise fuelled endorphins that were now gone. This turned me into a complete pain in the ass; mood swings, twitchy, stressed... like an irritable coiled spring. Jo and my family got serious points for putting up with me through that. Race week arrived and we flew to Nice. The nerves and worries were soothed by the view of my partly crushed bike box coming off the conveyor belt at the airport. Mid melt-down I opened it to find the frame was ok. Close call! Race registration and loosen up swim complete I'd spent much of the taper reading about how you should keep clear of the Ironman event village so you don't end up walking for miles and tiring yourself out the day before the big race. For me being as far away from this wallet raping circus wasn't difficult. It felt like a sea of expensive bits of plastic that probably wont make you faster and that you definitely don't need to buy. After my bike was checked into T1, I opted instead for a pizza and a chill out with Jo after doing a very light swim and a gentle jog along the front. Now to try and sleep! The long awaited race day arrived I woke up at 3:30am after a seriously patchy nights sleep. I ate my pre-race breakfast consisting bagel, Meridian Peanut butter, honey and a banana and washed it down with a cup of coffee. I walked down to T1, put my drink bottles on the bike and pumped up the tyres... All that was left was to get myself together. After nearly missing the race start after a nervous last minute porta-loo visit I made my way down to the beach and slotted myself into the 1hr 15min swim wave. I had no idea how long it might take me because I'd never swum this far and only clocked up two swim sessions this year. The gun went off and I ran into the sea and began to swim. God the water was clear! I felt surprisingly relaxed being surrounded by the sea of people and distracted myself by remembering to hum when my face was in the water. This was my reminder to exhale as I swam. It was the most surreal experience, looking down into the beautiful blue water of the Cote d'Azur one minute, then watching the most amazing sun rise over Nice as I turned my head to breathe. I kept swimming and the water turned from light blue to dark and then back to light blue again... I kept going until I noticed the shapes of the gravel appearing. I survived the swim and exited the water in 1 hr 14 minutes. Leaving the water. The day can only get better! After cocking up and leaving my race number belt in my transition bag and having to run back through transition to get it, I headed out onto the bike course still nervous about what was coming. I stuck to my self imposed 160bpm heart rate limit and seemed to be overtaking loads of other riders on the Col de l'Ecre. The ride was so picturesque and despite climbing 12,362ft it felt easy. I think I was so caught up in the drama and excitement of actually doing an Ironman the time passed quickly. The road narrowed as I headed back into Nice and came up on the back of another group of riders. Annoyingly they were riding 3 abreast in a mini peleton (I thought Ironman was a non-drafting race?!)... before I knew what was happening a motorbike marshal was beeping and waving a card at me shouting in French. My ski resort level French wasn't really on form after 2.4 miles of swimming and 112 miles of biking. Not really understanding what was going on I carried on into T2. I headed out onto the bike for the baptism of pain that is an Ironman Marathon... Sh*t I've left my Garmin on my bike! I was already out of transition and on the run course so I couldn't go back... I felt an odd calmness and carried on running... Looking back I think this experience was destined to be about feeling rather than being a slave to numbers. One lap down... 3 to go! I had become pretty comfortable in my iron run pace (around 7:30/mile) so I settled into that fairly quickly. Every time I ran past my family the hairs on my neck stood up and a lump in my throat appeared. The half of the run was a blur and passed in around 1hr 45mins. I felt ok and kept taking orange slices and gels at alternate feed stations. I ran through the end of lap 3 and picked up the yellow armband.... f*ck I can actually do this!!! Within 2 minutes of sliding that long awaited yellow armband on the fire and pain descended. My feet instantly felt like they were on fire. My quads felt like they had turned to pieces of wood that might split if I ran another step. The Ironman Nice run is a mentally difficult one because from each end of the run course you can see the other... and it looks bloody far! Running through the pain I spent the entire time shouting at myself, out loud, probably looking like I was nuttier than squirrel shit. Tears in the eyes I rounded the bend at the airport and just needed to make it back. Feeling like I was running on hot coals I supped down a flat coke and dug in, almost delirious from the pain... finally the turn to the finish line appeared and I stumbled over the line in 11 hours, 11 minutes and 11 seconds. I saw Jo and held my arms out and she said "you did it! you're an IRONMAN!!!!" accompanied by a wave of tears. My god how long I've wanted to hear those words. Finally! All the 1s! Despite looking like death, I couldn't be happier. 100% couldn't have done it without Jo I went for my post race massage and collected my t-shirt. The masseuse took off my trainers and revealed the reason that my feet were on fire... Look away if you're squeamish. Despite loosing skin and nails... nothing could take away how chuffed I was that I had this medal! For those numerology aficionados amongst you, seeing repeated 1s in a sequence, most commonly 1111 is a big big knock on the door from the universe to pay attention and wake up! Seeing all the 1s usually appears when you are about to go through a major awakening of some kind of change or shift[ (Look at this site if you're interested in reading more)](). Usually people only get four 1s.... Not really being known for doing things lightly I went for the 6! The months that followed Ironman Nice proved to be months of great change... Starting with getting fired when I got back to work. People often talk about the feeling of walking their path or their destiny... I never really understood that feeling until now.... ← Back to the blog Train with Horsepower If that is how you like your coaching, straight and built for your race, take a look at the training plans or see how coaching works . blog/f/ironman-wales---enter-the-dragon/.body: Skip to content ☰ Home Coached by Tom Female Performance Plan Only Plan Store About Us Blog Contact Blog / 25 January 2021 Ironman Wales - Enter The Dragon By Tom Cooling · 25 January 2021 So it's 11 days until Ironman Wales and the nerves and anticipation are starting to stir... I made the trip down to Tenby over the weekend to ride the bike route on my TT bike as a bit of a tester. I'd completed the course on my road bike last year and I needed to see how it would feel climbing on the bull horns on a bike built for flat out speed, not dancing up switchbacks. I'd set the bike up with my 40mm Easton EC70 SL training wheels and the nutrition/ hydration setup I was intending to use on race day. The idea being that I'd spin around the course like this, be able to practice fuelling as I will during the race but when I switch onto my race wheelset and aero helmet, I might find a bit of free speed. The Argon E112 in training mode I headed out onto the bike course feeling surprised to see loads of other people out on the route making the most of the good bank holiday weekend weather and getting one last look at the bike course that is widely regarded as one of the toughest on the Ironman race circuit. The thing that makes the Ironman Wales bike course so challenging isn't the number of feet climbed, at only 7,365ft (according to my strava from last year's Ironman Wales) it comes in nearly 5,000ft short of the Ironman Nice bike course. The thing that makes it so hard is the way those climbs appear, the route profile is a bit like looking into the mouth of a crocodile... none of the teeth are that big but there are so many of them... Endless short steep climbs that suck the life from your legs with no real opportunity to get into a rhythm and keep the effort level constant. My benchmark was last year's race where I got around the bike course in 5 hours and 55 minutes. Since then I've managed to add nearly 50 watts to my one hour power or FTP. I tapped these figures into Best Bike Split to suss out a bit of a race plan as I had no idea how to tackle this jagged beast.... The survey says??? ding ding ding... For a 77% intensity factor I need to average 235 watts and keep my normalised power below 250 watts. This should hopefully get me back to Tenby without blowing up and with something left for the equally challenging run course. We shall see how easy keeping it under control is when the crowds on the infamous 'Heartbreak Hill' in Saundersfoot are roaring, almost beckoning you into the red... Ironman Wales 2016 - Heartbreak Hill in Saundersfoot - The wrong side of my heart rate limit! Out on the course this wattage target felt pretty achievable. I realised I need to be more flexible with the plan than just sitting at my average wattage target and let myself stray up towards 300w on some of the climbs. I completed one complete loop of the course averaging 20mph and felt pretty good. We'll see how that pans out on race day... After I'd finished my recce I rolled back into Tenby and got a bit of a re-fuel before heading down to the beach for an odd opportunity to walk the swim course thanks to the tide being peak low. This was pretty good as it gave me a chance to confirm my sighting targets and break the swim leg down in my head. So now the taper begins... commence battling with too much free time to worry about what helmet to wear, not getting ill, flitting between race strategies, worrying about the amount of prep I've done. I think I should probably sit back and focus on the last 12 months of quality training I've put in and know that it will see me ok come race day. After all, like Morpheus says; ← Back to the blog Train with Horsepower If that is how you like your coaching, straight and built for your race, take a look at the training plans or see how coaching works . blog/f/make-the-plan-then-hold-it/index..body: Skip to content ☰ Home Coached by Tom Female Performance Plan Only Plan Store About Us Blog Contact Blog / 10 August 2026 Make the Plan, Then Have the Discipline to Hold It By Tom Cooling · 10 August 2026 The race is usually lost in the first hour, and it's lost by feeling good. You're fresh, the legs are singing, everyone around you is going hard, and the plan that told you to hold back suddenly feels far too cautious. So you spend a little extra, and a little more, and by the back half you're paying it all back with interest. A race plan is only worth anything if you've got the discipline to hold it when it feels wrong to. Why do people blow up when they had a plan? Because a plan is a promise you make to yourself when you're calm, and you break it when you're excited. The physiology isn't complicated. Go above your sustainable intensity early and you tip into burning through glycogen and piling up fatigue faster than you can clear it. It feels free at the time because you're fresh. It is not free. It's a loan, and the interest rate is brutal in the last third. The riders who execute aren't tougher or fitter than the ones who fold. They're just more disciplined in the opening hour, when discipline is hardest and matters most. Should you hold constant power the whole way? No, and this is where a lot of simple advice goes wrong. Holding one flat number isn't how I pace a real course, because a real course isn't flat. The right pacing is variable power, spent where it buys you the most time, and constrained so the whole effort still adds up to the same total. The way I set it up: On sustained climbs, spend a little more. On a climb steeper than about three per cent, you can lift the power to around eight per cent over target. You're moving slowly here, so the extra watts buy a lot of time. On descents, back right off. On anything steeper than about minus three per cent, drop to around eighty-eight per cent of target or just spin. You're already fast; extra watts here buy you almost nothing, so bank the energy. Into a headwind, a small lift. Headwind sections take a touch more, in the region of three to four per cent, because that's where you're slowest for the effort. It all has to renormalise. This is the non-negotiable bit. The whole plan is normalised back to your target intensity, so the redistribution makes you faster on the same energy. It's never a licence to spend extra energy dressed up as clever pacing. Same budget, spent smarter. The caps get smaller the longer the race. A short time trial has headroom to play with; an Ironman bike leg does not, so the swings shrink accordingly. Why does spending on the climbs and saving on the descents make you faster? It comes down to where your watts turn into time. On a climb you're moving slowly, so most of your effort is going into hauling you up the hill against gravity, and gravity doesn't care how aerodynamic you are. A few extra watts there translate into a meaningful chunk of time saved, because you're spending a long time on that stretch. On a fast descent the opposite is true. You're already moving quickly, air resistance is enormous and rising with the cube of your speed, so pouring watts in buys you almost nothing; you'd burn a lot of energy to gain a couple of seconds. The intelligent move is to take that same energy and spend it where it's cheap to buy time, which is the climbs, and coast where time is expensive to buy, which is the descents. That's the whole logic of variable pacing. It's not about working harder overall, it's about moving the same total effort to the parts of the course where it pays. Constant power feels disciplined but it's actually leaving time on the road, because it spends the same on a descent, where watts are wasted, as on a climb, where they're gold. What about wind, heat and fuelling? These aren't footnotes. They change the actual numbers on the day. Wind changes what a given speed costs. A plan built for still air is wrong the moment the forecast turns, so the pacing has to account for the wind you'll actually meet, section by section. Heat raises your heart rate for the same power, pushes your fluid and electrolyte losses up, and quietly lowers the intensity you can hold. Pretending it doesn't is how people cook themselves by halfway. Fuelling is the one that ends more races than fitness does. You can't pace a plan you haven't fuelled. If the carbohydrate isn't going in from early, the back half of the plan is fiction, because the engine has nothing left to spend. When I write a race plan for one of my athletes, I build these in, so the plan is for the day you're actually racing, not an idealised one. But the plan only sets the targets. You still have to execute them. How do you actually hold back early? You decide, before the start, that the first hour is going to feel too easy, and you treat that feeling as confirmation you're doing it right, not a sign to push. You watch your own numbers, not the people around you, because you don't know their plan or their fitness and half of them are making the exact mistake you're trying to avoid. And you trust that the discipline you show in the first hour is precisely what buys you the freedom to race hard in the last one. Make the plan honestly. Fuel it. Hold it when it feels wrong. That's the whole game, and the hardest part of it happens when you still feel great. ← Back to the blog Train with Horsepower If that is how you like your coaching, straight and built for your race, take a look at the training plans or see how coaching works .
