blog/f/my-triathlon-top-tips/index.html.body: Skip to content ☰ Home Coached by Tom Female Performance Plan Only Plan Store About Us Blog Contact Blog / 25 January 2021 My Triathlon Top Tips By Tom Cooling · 25 January 2021 So since Covid-19 is trying to derail any hopes of a long race season in 2021, I thought it was worth sharing a few of my top 10 triathlon mistakes to make sure you hit the ground running when you can toe the start line. Every single one of these was unfortunately learned the hard way so this is your golden opportunity to learn from someone else's mistakes rather than doing them yourself. Tip #1 The 7 P's Proper, prior, preparation, prevents, piss, poor, performance ... There are a few different versions but I like this one the most. It's probably fair to say you could rock up at a triathlon with no prep and just see how it goes and if you're already fit you might do very well. But the thing that differentiates triathlon from most other sports is the fact you're dealing with 3 different disciplines, multiple pieces of equipment/footwear/clothing, event specific procedures and rules, getting some good quality preparation in before the event reduces the likelihood you will be tripped up by something silly and ruin your chances of a PB. One of the best ways to learn more about triathlon is to join a club, there you can share knowledge with other athletes. You can use the club search tool on British Triathlon to find one . Get a Training Plan - Understanding the kind of training, the quantity of training and the intensity of that training isn't easy. It sounds obvious, but speaking from my own training/coaching experience, most people will avoid the training they find difficult and revert to the stuff they like or that makes them feel good. Annoyingly the things they find hard are usually the ones that will make them better. Getting a plan will help you understand what an effective plan should look like, but that is only a 2 dimensional image. Read on to find out how to go 3D. There are plenty of athletes who have reached great success being self coached, but get a good coach and they can help make your triathlon journey much more enjoyable by guiding you through the pitfalls of multisport. Part of the benefit of getting a coach is to have someone understand you and design a training plan around your life and target event. Getting that specificity and volume right can make all the difference in success or failure. But for me the main benefit of being coached is being accountable to someone and having someone look at your training and progress objectively. This is something that's almost impossible to do for yourself and is the reason although I'm a coach, I'm being coached for my main event in 2021. You can get in touch with any triathlon training or preparation questions here. Hot Tip - Either enter a warm up race or if you can't, arrange a mini event where you trial all of the kit, equipment and nutrition you aim to use on race day. Tip #2 - Don't be a Magpie Although for an athlete, triathlon is a journey of self improvement and a quest to overcome adversity, its important we all understand how big business triathlon is... in 2015 the global triathlon market was worth £8.6billion. We've all see race entry fees skyrocket in the last few years so I'd hate to imagine what that number is now. All you need to do is buy your favourite triathlon magazine or log onto any triathlon related website and you'll see endless adverts for the new and shiny piece of tri equipment or clothing that is sure to shave seconds, minutes or hours off your personal best. I definitely wont deny there are pieces of kit that can make your life better and possibly make you faster, but there are three things that are almost certainly going to make you faster and give you more consistent performances in triathlon: 1. Using kit that fits you, kit that you know and kit you trust (it doesn't have to be new) - Thinking back to Ironman Nice in 2016. I got suckered in to buying a new set of socks because of their supposed magic compression, foot cooling, fatigue reducing ability... I'd worn these once for some taper runs going into the event and opted to roll with them on the run. I ended up losing most of the skin on my feet when they duly turned into cheese graters half way around the marathon. Not fun. 2. Saving your money and training a bit more - I'd bet anyone reading this if any time they nearly bought a new bit of kit they stopped and did an hour of zone 2 running or cycling, by their next race they would crush their PB. 3. The day before the event, register then steer well clear of the event village. The amount of time you'll spend on your feet wondering around looking at new and shiny will do nothing for a strong performance the day after. Do your prep sessions, get home to rest, rehydrate and refuel. Most importantly remember why you're there and all the sacrifices you've made to get you to that point where you're poised to crush that race. Tired Legs + New Kit = Slow Racing & Sore Feet Rested and Refuelled body + Calm Focussed Mind = Fast Racing & PBs Tip #3 - Be Hungry That leads me neatly on to talking about being hungry. Now I'm not talking about food, I'm talking about psychology. One thing I've seen from my own journey as an athlete and coach is how bad triathletes are at resting and taking a physical or mental break from the sport. Ask yourself, how many times have worried “What if I lose my fitness during a break?" or "Will all of my hard work will be wasted if I take a day off?” Now you might be wondering, why is he talking about being hungry and then going on about taking time off but I'll tell you one thing I've seen from my own journey as an athlete and coach is how bad age group triathletes are at resting and taking a physical or mental break from the sport. If you speak to any professional triathlete, taking a real break in the winter is crucial to succeeding in the following season. Your body and mind just needs the time to absorb and reset. Its highly likely that you will come back from a mini break less fresh but no less fit. I was once told its better to turn up to a race 10% less fit than 1% over-trained. At the time I didn't really understand it until I actually turned up at a race over-trained and psychologically burnt out. This has shaped the way I think about training and coaching because I now put a value on hungriness in a similar way to everyone is fixated on their CTL (chronic training load) in Training Peaks. One thing I think most coaches miss, is understanding that to get the best out of someone, they need to be up for the fight with psychological capacity/freshness to go deep and keep the pressure on at the painful back end of a race. So this tip is about listening to yourself and recognising when you need to back off in order to go forward stronger. Tip #4 Don't Follow the Herd This one links to the above point about being hungry. Its all too easy to see what everyone else is doing and try to do the same. This might be because you don't want to get left behind or doubt your own direction. What I'm telling you is you are most likely different and might need something different in order for you to succeed. Have courage to strike out on your own. I've got two examples of this that I've lived so hopefully you can apply it to yourself. 1. Kit So as background I've been a bike mechanic since I was 15 so I know how to adjust a front mech, but I've always hated them. Everyone will have experienced that sinking feeling of hitting a hill, dropping down to the small ring only for the chain to unceremoniously drop into that endless chasm between the crank and your frame leaving you at a standstill. Riding a 2x (two-by / two front chainrings) is a bit of an art when you're coming at it from a variability index perspective (riding smoothly by keeping your normalised power as close to your average power as possible). Being able to move the rear cassette in preparation for the chainring shift to keep your cadence smooth. When I saw narrow wide chainrings come out and Sram pushing 1x on MTB and off-road I thought "hold up, what if I used that for triathlon??". What if you could choose a single chainring and cassette combo that would give you the same range as a 2x setup so you can still go as fast and climb as easily, but you only have to worry about one gear lever. Wouldn't that be more simple. My coach at the time thought it wouldn't work as did many other athletes who clocked my setup in transition but I knew that my intended race (Ironman Wales) had such a choppy and changing bike course, having a smooth simple gearing system would be a dream to ride. Now anyone who knows that bike course and knows about variability index will know, riding it smoothly is hard. I rode my 1x TT bike at 1.05 variability index ending up with a 5hr 32minute bike time. The case was closed and a big big win for 1x. More than happy for anyone to get in touch to talk through 1x and its application for triathlon racing. 2. Training & Intensity Now Covid has stranded most of us in our homes so training has largely migrated into the virtual world. Now I LOVE Zwift, Rouvy and anything that breaks the boredom of turbo time and gives you an opportunity to scratch that competitive itch but I think it might actually turn out to be a thorn in many budding triathletes side. In the last few months I've seen a massive momentum toward racing regularly on Zwift, this is something that should be celebrated but also treated with caution. Being part of a team and racing community is a great way of beating Covid lockdown blues and something I thoroughly enjoyed in the summer, but it also might be the fast lane to overtraining. I don't necessarily agree that excessive racing this time of the year is the best thing for me or my athletes. Purely because being super fit at Easter isn't going to help you get around an Ironman in September if you've blown your doors by July. Again, this is just an example of listening to your body, listening to your coach and understanding what is right for you. Tip #5 - Be Calm As I've already touched on, triathlon is tough. Its tough because you need to be good at three sports at once to succeed, its tough because you're relying on multiple pieces of equipment and clothing to get around the course, and then there is the big big variable of everyone else racing, the weather on the day, the road surface on the bike course... the list goes on and on. This tip is a bit more anecdotal but was something I learned in my A race of 2018. I'd decided to go big and took on a pro level training program in the hope of achieving a dream... the illusive sub 10 hour finish at Ironman Wales. I'd turned up overtrained and a bit burned out, but I was fit. The swim went smoothly with no kit failure or incidents in the water... still on target. The lengthy run from the beach to T1 was fine and went as well as could be expected... still on target. I dropped my swim stuff and got into my bike kit including a pair of arm warmers because it was pretty nippy... I grabbed my bike and started running to the T1 exit when I noticed my arm warmer wasn't pulled up. I tried to remedy this while running. All of a sudden the front wheel turned and the bike went down on its side... my BTA (between the arms) bottle that had all of my energy gels poured into it opened up and emptied out onto the tarmac before I could pick the bike up.... In the heat of the moment I just grabbed the bike, jumped on and began my assault on the bike course. I certainly wasn't calm and problem solving on the fly... I carried on riding past feed stops holding my target race power... It wasn't long before the dreaded bonk appeared and I went from 18th overall to more like 100th. I ended up almost collapsing into a feed stop at 85miles on the bike course to refuel. What I should have done is stopped at the first feed stop on the bike course. Accepted I'd lose a little bit of time grabbing enough nutrition to see me the whole way through the course instead of blindly riding on. That silly oversight cost me my dream finish. Something I'd rather avoid happening to any of you. The key with triathlon isn't necessarily being the fittest, sometimes it comes down to who can problem solve on the fly and keep going. Be calm, keep thinking and just maybe you'll get the race result you want. Tip #6 - Be Humble My last tip is about being humble. When you're dealing with something as uncertain as multisport, being anything other than humble is a sure fire way to trip yourself up and look like a tit. I think there is a key transition for competitive triathletes when they stop thinking so much about everyone else who is racing on the day and turn up focussed on racing themselves. Everyone dreams of an age group or overall finish position, but the thing I've learned is there is always someone faster. You need to focus on the variables that are in your control and try to forget the ones out of your control. That is really the only way to consistently achieve a positive race outcome. That positive race outcome might equate to an age group or overall position, but don't make that your focus. The other thing about this sport is the sacrifice you have to make to get in shape to participate. There are always people around you supporting you on that journey, be it family or friends and its worth remembering them and how your journey might impact their lives. I hope this list of tips has been helpful. It's probably not the type of list you might have imagined reading about but I think its a list of things that every triathlete should remember. Happy to chat through any thoughts or answer any questions about any of the other content. Feel free to contact me here. ← Back to the blog Train with Horsepower If that is how you like your coaching, straight and built for your race, take a look at the training plans or see how coaching works . blog/f/once-twice-three-times-an-ironman.body: Skip to content ☰ Home Coached by Tom Female Performance Plan Only Plan Store About Us Blog Contact Blog / 25 January 2021 Once, Twice, Three Times an Ironman By Tom Cooling · 25 January 2021 It's 4 days since Ironman Wales and the whole weekend is beginning to sink in. I turned up in Tenby looking to seek a bit of justice after what felt like a complete failure in Alpe d'Huez. My plan was pretty simple; Get the swim done and onto the bike by the time 1 hour and 10 minutes had elapsed. Get back from the ride with no more than 6 hours 30 minutes on the clock. Survive the run hoping I had enough of a time buffer from the bike to keep me in the Kona slot places. My target finish time was as close to 10 hours as I could manage with a 9 something finish time, a bit of a hush hush dream. You might read this and think nah that's never going to happen in Tenby but the sad truth of it was within the last few weeks of training before taper I'd logged a 61 minute 4000 meter open water swim and a few days after comfortably rode the Ironman Wales bike course at 20 mph with the TT bike in full training spec (training wheels and vented helmet). Admittedly I haven't put in anywhere near the required run volume to be able to put together a quick Ironman marathon but I thought I could hang on to a 3 hours 30 minute split if I was at the sharp end of my age group. So we headed down to Tenby on Saturday morning to get checked into our hotel and register for the race. I was refreshing the Met Office website every 10 minutes to see what was happening with the weather... the forecast - incredibly unsettled with high winds likely. I'd managed to book me and the family into hotels on the Esplanade overlooking the finish line, a very good choice in terms of proximity to the transition area and a very short walk to your bed at the end of the race. After a little mooch around Tenby showing my family where the good spectating spots were, race registration, bike check in and a go on the NormaTec Recovery boots at the Ironman expo I was ready for a pizza and bed and headed back to the Hotel for some downtime. I slept very well and woke up calm and ready to go, ate my usual pre-race breakfast and headed to transition at 5 am to give the bike one last check over and load up my water bottles. I was pleasantly surprised that at this point in the morning the weather was calm and wind was low... I couldn't believe we had lucked out with a clear day... how wrong I way. One of the best parts of competing in Ironman Wales is the national anthem before the race start. Even if you're not remotely patriotic, the sound of thousands of people singing the anthem in such a beautiful location will get you blubbing! A few minutes later the gun horn blows and the race is underway. Swim I ran into the sea making sure I kept to the right of the archway so I had a bit of clear water. With my most recent 4km swim performance in mind I seeded myself in the 57 minute swim group hoping that I could hold my own. I focused on swimming a smooth and rhythmic stroke and the first lap passed without incident. I hit the Australian exit in 33 minutes and headed out for the second lap. This was a good few minutes behind where I wanted to be. Thinking about it I wonder if I was consciously swimming at an easier pace to avoid a panic attack as happened in Alpe d'Huez... who knows. Onto the second lap and the water had changed... yes it was still cold (around 17 degrees apparently) but had a great deal more swell. The swim out to the first buoy seemed to take forever, almost like I was swimming through treacle. I finally made it back to the beach and stopped the watch.... 1 hour 9 minutes?! What?! I ran up the beach pulling off my wetsuit, I dealt with a quick flash of cramp in my left quad and jumped into my running shoes to head through town to T1... Bike As soon as I got out of T1 onto the bike course I was 100% pleased that I'd taken the time to stick on some arm warmers. The cold swim had sapped my body heat and with the constant wind hitting my body as I rode, the shivers began. The IM Wales bike course is tight, technical and hilly with a mix of smooth and rough road surfaces. It consists of two loops, one 70 miles and the second 40 miles. The first section of the big loop is fast and lets you build up a good average speed before hitting the technical sections that are to come... I say fast, but definitely not today! The wind was absolutely howling in from the Atlantic making everyone around me twitchy as hell. Every time I approached a gap in the hedge, our only shelter from the wind, I saw other riders swing wildly across the road. This made overtaking a very dangerous endeavour. In addition to the twitchy riders, the road was narrow, twisty, and covered in fallen leaves. Danger bells were ringing on every descent. This highlighted a bit of a fear I've got with descending in anything other than bone dry conditions. A few years ago I had a nasty stack on some ice and since then, anytime I'm pressing on downhill I end up visualising the bike sliding out from underneath me... not ideal when you're trying to keep your head in the game. A few miles later on some of the tricky tight descents, marshals holding big signs saying "OIL ON ROAD!" were out in the road shouting at us to slow down... this did nothing for my confidence and made the bike leg a game of survival. Finally I'd made it to Saundersfoot. By this point my tri-suit was completely saturated and I wasn't sure how much longer I could push on feeling that cold plus the fatigue in my upper back from bracing against the wind for the last few hours wasn't helping either. I knew Heart Break hill meant big crowds and a chance to light up the burners to try and get some heat back in the oven. I hit the bottom of the climb, up out of the saddle and treated myself to a little 400w blast... much to the delight of the hardy supporters that were out braving the rain to cheer us on! https://www.instagram.com/p/BY58G42jKb8/?hl=en The one thing that really ground on me the entire route was the constant string of riders drafting. The motorbike marshals didn't seem to care as people hitched on for a free ride. My enemy on the bike was bib # 315... a fella wearing full Russian team kit who decided to hang onto the back of me for 105 miles before overtaking on the way back into Tenby with what I'm sure were very fresh legs. It was like a scene that Icarus doping/ cheating documentary. I rolled back into Tenby with a 5 hour 55 minute bike split. .. a cool 30 minutes behind my desired target time. I knew I'd been holding back a lot to get around safely but looking down at my bike computer revealed my average power was only 213 watts and intensity factor down at 73%. Morale at this point was pretty low because I knew my hopes of a Kona spot were out of the window unless I turned into Haile Gebrselassie... pretty unlikely at this stage in an Ironman. Run Out onto the run course and my legs felt good... they bloody should have after riding the bike with an intensity factor 8% lower than my race plan. My run load this year was pretty short and focused on speed work as I'd concentrated on 70.3 distance events all year so I knew I wasn't going to be breaking any records even with a gentle effort on the bike. Tip tapping out of Tenby heading up the climb for the first time I was doing the maths in my head.... 'so if I hold for a 3 hour 26 minute run split I could still make a 10 hour 45 minute finish...'. My legs still felt pretty good so I tried to stick to this plan and hold an average of 7 minutes 52/mile. The first two laps ticked by smoothly and I collected a blue and green armband on my wrist. I knew the fatigue was going to come, I just didn't know when. My furthest run this year was the 13.2 mile run leg of the Brecon Titan half Ironman in June. I think I've averaged 15 miles a week since then so was in no way marathon fit. POW! The third time I hit the road climbing out of Tenby and my legs just said no. I stopped and had to take a seat at the side of the road munching on crisps and drinking flat coke. I couldn't stand the idea of anymore sugar so headed for the savoury stuff. I gave myself a bit of a mental kick up the arse and started running again when I remembered I could still make it home in under 11 hours if I could get my pace back up. This pace chart tells the story; plain sailing until mile 14 when I was reduced to the crisp raid. I finally made it back into Tenby and supported by the roaring crowds who's throats must have been sore from what was then 11 hours of shouting (GO TENBY!!!) rounded the last bend onto the Esplanade. The finish line was in sight and I was more than pleased to see it. I took a bit more time and enjoyed the experience of running down the red carpet high-fiving people as I went. https://www.instagram.com/p/BY6ZXEnj6-P/?hl=en No arms raised or smiles when I crossed the line. Just a bit of a lull and disappointment. My finish time was 11 hours, 10 minutes and 28 seconds. A new Iron distance personal best and just under 10 minutes faster than I managed in Tenby last year, despite the significantly worse conditions. Something to be happy about? I'm not really sure. I'm just a bit annoyed. I have some points to be happy about and some key points for improvement if I'm going to realise my potential next year; I need to race in some open water swims so I can get a grip with both swimming close to other people and pacing. This should get me out onto the bike course with some clearer roads. I need to master the flying mount on the bike. My transitions are fast but there are free seconds there for the taking! My nutrition strategy on the bike is good and kept me feeling strong throughout the ride. I need to increase my run load so I can race the Ironman marathon rather than just survive it. I need to improve my run leg nutrition strategy. I definitely under-fuelled this one leading to the mile 14 bonk. I just want to say a big big thank you to both my family (Jo, Mum, Huw, Nan & Nick) who came down to support me in a very wet and windy Tenby. Thank you to each and every member of my Ironman Fan club who were there in spirit and to the absolutely amazing crowds in Tenby and the surrounding villages who braved the rain to keep everyone's morale up and make Ironman Wales the best on the Ironman calendar. ← Back to the blog Train with Horsepower If that is how you like your coaching, straight and built for your race, take a look at the training plans or see how coaching works . blog/f/our-origins---a-little-bit-of-his.body: Skip to content ☰ Home Coached by Tom Female Performance Plan Only Plan Store About Us Blog Contact Blog / 25 January 2021 Origins - A Little Bit of History By Tom Cooling · 25 January 2021 After a solid bump back down to earth at the Alpe d’Huez triathlon last week I thought putting my thoughts into words might provide me with some means of processing it all and you with some comedy plus maybe a guide to help you on your triathlon journey. How about some context… despite starting off as a really active child and running cross country at primary school, I didn’t enter my first race until I was 23. I spent most of my youth messing around on a skateboard until I was old enough to buy a car… then it was all about going fast on 4 wheels. At 22 I knew I needed a challenge and after 9 months in the Royal Marines and two bouts of UK Special Forces selection, I learned three things; I could iron with the best of them, I didn’t want to get told what to do for a living and I loved pushing myself past the limit. The infamous 984 “Sunshine” Troop – Famous for never getting rained on in the field. Leaving the Marines was THE biggest shock. After feeling like a piece of steel that could take any weather, any weight and any arduous task on the chin I found myself among a sea of lean, Lycra-clad runners. I had the mistaken belief that after what I’d just been through in the Commando Training Center, Lympstone that I’d be able to “smash all these civvies, no dramas”… The gun went off at the 2009 Monmouth Kymin Dash, a hilly run consisting of a 7 mile loop with one 899ft climb, and these civvies dropped me like a bad habit. I gritted through and finished 24th out of the 150 runners. One fast civvie….. probably twice my age. Needless to say, getting smashed by civvies didn’t sit very well with me at all… I began Rocky Balboa-esque training, I wanted to be better, I just didn’t know at what… My passion for this addiction grew and grew until it started rubbing off on other people. I would use the 899ft Kymin hill climb as a proving ground for any would be training partners. I figured if they have the heart to complete that climb without cracking then they might be fit (or stubborn) enough to make the cut. Little did I know, dragging my best mate Richy Bowen up this climb would give me a great training partner and a fearsome adversary. Just about holding Richy off at the finish line – May Hill Massacre 2011 We started training at our local gym trying to complete workouts I had devised with making us sick as the general ethos. Leaving the gym we would peer down into the sports hall to watch the local Circuit Training Club muttering “pussies” under our breath. Looking for a change I bit the bullet and joined the Circuit Training club and found a whole new way to bury myself. The day after my first session my body hurt everywhere but I was hooked. It was at circuits that I met Mike Bennett, a coach who turned into a great friend. Me, Mike & Deano… The Circuit Training tripod at the final session in our old gym Years passed like this… 3 vomit-inducing batterings at circuits plus the odd run and a race thrown in every now and then. I was strong and fit and I used to see value in being able to race and finish in the top 10% without taking training or my diet very seriously. This is something I regret because I now know there is no value in being a mediocre you when the best you is hiding behind a few more hours of hard work. 2012 Newport Marathon – 2nd Place When I left the Marines I told myself that I would do an Ironman one day… I thought the Ironman was THE hardest event you could do as a civilian and thought it would be the only thing that could fill the gap the Marines had left… It wasn’t until 3 years later that I got my first chance to taste triathlon. I had been swimming with my local triathlon club when they attempted to put on a Sprint distance race in Monmouth. This consisted of a 400m pool swim, 15 mile hilly bike and a 3 mile flat run. I signed up straight away. I knew my swim was by far my weakest discipline, my bike good and my run strong. At this point I had absolutely no concept of pacing and would head out at a completely unsustainable Prefontaine-esque pace and hope to hang on to the finish through the painful lactic acid fueled blur… Riding my 10kg road bike and wearing Nike Waffle Racers, a broken tri-suit and a race t-shirt from the previous year’s Kymin Dash I set about attacking the course. I went out far too big on the ride but thankfully the course was short enough that it didn’t bite back. I just about held on for the run and thanks to a bit of natural running strength I crossed the line in 11th position, the highest finish of all the Monmouth Triathlon Club members…not bad for my first outing in multi-sport. ← Back to the blog Train with Horsepower If that is how you like your coaching, straight and built for your race, take a look at the training plans or see how coaching works . blog/f/plastic-pollution-triathlon/index.body: Skip to content ☰ Home Coached by Tom Female Performance Plan Only Plan Store About Us Blog Contact Blog / 25 January 2021 Plastic Plastic Plastic - A Story About Sport & Plastic Pollution By Tom Cooling · 25 January 2021 The knock at the door... 16-20 energy gel wrappers 8 water bottles 3 plastic transition bags plastic athlete wristband plastic packaging on that thing you panic bought in the days leading up to the race that will save you 10 seconds.... That was just for me at my last punt at Ironman Wales in 2017. If you multiply those figures by the circa 3000 athletes racing, you end up with some pretty big numbers indeed; 60,000 gel wrappers - 24,000 water bottles - 9,000 plastic transition bags That is without even taking into account the water bottles, coffee cups, food wrappers etc that the spectators at the event produced... The journey... Dropped here... Confused for food here... Dies here. Whats The Problem? Well sadly there are a lot of us, humans I mean and through combination of laziness and time crunched lifestyles we pick lifestyle choices that tend to create a lot of waste. In 1950s, the worlds population was roughly 2.5 billion people... back then we produced 1.5 million tonnes of plastic. In 2016 that population increased to 7 billion people who produced a whopping 320 million tonnes of plastic. Surfers Against Sewage suggest this will double by 2034. Plastic is great, it's strong, flexible and durable...but it can last for 450 years in a marine environment. This plastic slowly fragments into smaller and smaller pieces that are eventually eaten by the smallest marine organisms who are in turn eaten by slightly bigger organisms again and again and again until the point where fish that feature in our food chain such as your cod, mackerel or snapper, have a stomach full of it. 1 in 3 fish that are caught for human consumption now contain plastic. Plastic which has been acting like a magnet to cancer causing chemicals the entire time it's been floating about. Just consider this... by 2050 there will be more plastic in the sea than fish ( Ellen MacArthur Foundation ). What are you going to have for your high protein lunch then? A plastic bottle and quinoa? (Ellen MacArthur Foundation) Triathletes spend countless hours training their bodies, eating clean and honing their performance so on race day they can go for the win or the PB of their dreams. Do we really think that eating food laced with plastic and chemicals a good foundation for our performance? All caused by us not being able to spend a few pounds on a keep cup for that coffee you need after a big session, or remembering to take a water bottle with you rather than buying a plastic one because you feel a bit dehydrated. Laziness is the killer people. It just takes some thought, a little bit of time and a tiny bit of preparation and I'd bet you that you could cut out at least 50% of the plastic waste you produce a week. Why This Is Important To Me? So over last winter I was lucky enough to travel to Indonesia and West Papua to learn to scuba dive and assist with a marine conservation project. Now this place place was like a dream, like something from one of those 10 places you need to go before you die. It has been dubbed THE epicentre for marine biodiversity and is one of the last places on earth you can see live coral. I remember being at 29 meters deep at a dive site called Blue Magic. This dive site is in a deep channel located an hour boat ride from any form of civilisation. I was sat there watching a beautiful Oceanic Manta Ray cruise by and I turned around to see 3 plastic bags and a pink coat hanger. I just felt angry... angry that not everyone could see that something as trivial as accepting a plastic bag in a shop or a straw in a bar is ruining one of the true remaining wonders of the world. It wasn't just at depth that plastic was to be found. On every beach at every high tide another wave of plastic arrived. Straws, cups, flipflops, lighters, toothbrushes, rope, earbuds, bottles, bags... the list goes on... This is what laziness causes! Now I bet the number of triathletes queuing up to ditch the plastic would increase 100% if I told you that reducing your plastic footprint would make you 10% faster. Well actually I am saying that! I believe choosing to lead a more considered existence with a lower plastic footprint will make you faster. How you say? Like this; By thinking a bit more about good quality nutrition and preparing your meals you are less likely to buy those faddy plastic wrapped snacks. Ask yourself, do you really need to buy a small plastic packet of nuts and berries when you can buy them in bulk from a health food store for a fraction of the price. Get yourself a good quality "keep cup". That way you can still get the flat white caffeine fix to make it through your swim session and pay less for it thanks to the coffee shops offering a discount if you bring your own cup. Buy a reusable water bottle. By having a refillable vessel you will be able to stay on top of your hydration and wont need to buy bottled water. Dehydration = lower performance. Refilling your bottle is should be free (check out Refill.org for more info!) so you're saving money there. So by ditching plastic I've saved you money, fed you better, kept you caffeinated and improved your hydration. Tell me how that wont make you faster! Oh and before I forget you've cut your disposable plastic footprint by a huge percentage. Cool Ideas... So I'm already heavily invested in going low plastic but there are a few areas that I think I can improve; At the start of the blog I mentioned energy gels. For me this is my go to source of energy for Ironman racing. I usually buy packs of gels then work out how many I need for the race, empty them into my drinks bottles and water down. This leaves me with sometimes 20 plastic gel packets that cant be recycled. So I know I need 415g of carbohydrate for my 5 hour 30 minute bike split at Ironman Wales. At the moment this comes in the form of 16 gels but after much researching I've found that a 3:1 ratio combination of Honey (82g carbs per 100ml) and Blackstrap Molasses (74g carbs per 100ml) would give me everything I need. The recipe for each of my 750ml water bottles looks like this; Honey - 189ml Blackstrap Molasses - 70ml Water = 491ml Simple , clean and and natural organic energy. Zero plastic waste and much cheaper than energy gels. I've trialled this on several long intense rides and it works just as well as the energy gels. Plastic Heroes I raced the Immortal Sports Wimbleball Half Iron distance triathlon last month. I wanted to give them a shout-out for running a zero plastic hydration station on the bike and run legs. Although it took some time to stop and refill your own bottle, everyone had to do it and we saved a huge amount of plastic waste being produced. It's the little things that count! I participated in the Wheels in Wheels Forest of Dean Spring Classic Sportive in May. They provided zero plastic fixing straps to use when fixing your race number to your bike. This must have saved over 2000 plastic cable ties being wasted. Kudos! Big shout out to Finisterre for launching their Microplastics Collection. These are all made from Econyl , a fabric made from regenerated Nylon from our oceans and landfills. Not only do the pro cycling Team Sky have a Welsh man who is faster than me on a bike, they've also taken plastic pollution to arguably the biggest stage in professional sport. Check out Team Sky's Ocean Rescue initiative! To quote a good friend of mine...."if we all do a little bit more, everyone can do a little bit less". Do your bit towards reducing plastic pollution and lets clean up triathlon!!!! (and go faster in the process!!!!) ← Back to the blog Train with Horsepower If that is how you like your coaching, straight and built for your race, take a look at the training plans or see how coaching works . blog/f/psychology---use-your-head/index..body: Skip to content ☰ Home Coached by Tom Female Performance Plan Only Plan Store About Us Blog Contact Blog / 25 January 2021 Psychology - Use Your Head By Tom Cooling · 25 January 2021 So we're 4 days until Ironman Wales... the tension, excitement and anxiety are building and at this late stage in the game there is a quiet calmness because you know nothing more can be done to improve your physical performance. All of the hard training sessions have been banked and now while the body takes time to process and absorb the hours you've put in... you mind starts to wander. This is the bit where the question marks start appearing, where you start asking yourself if you've done enough, are you good enough, can you do it, can you hold your target pace and power, do you have the right kit, what will the weather be, why is EVERYONE in the office ill?!!!?! The list goes on... Many of these questions you just can't answer, many you don't need to but if you've done your preparation then many of the answers you'll already know. It's just the little seed of doubt that makes you question yourself... The fear of failure; what if things don't work out? The fear of success; what if things do work out and I can't handle it? This feels especially apparent to me this year because my list of fears is different to my first Ironman in Nice where I didn't know if I could make it around the course. I'm now sat here knowing that I have the ability to ride an age group winning bike split and run an age group winning run... but what if I don't? What if I don't put in a performance that will do myself justice, a performance that shows those closest to me that all of the times I've said "no I can't do that" or "I can't go there because I'm training" have been worth it. What that subtle change has taught me is fear doesn't go away. Fear is like perspective, it changes as you change. As a rule, your mind will always find something new to worry about no matter what you're doing... maybe this is an inherent human weakness. Are You Sitting Comfortably? You shouldn't be. Your dream should scare the sh*t out of you. It should both instil a deep fear but give you tingles of excitement at the same time. The thing with pushing yourself and doing big things is trying to manage fear, self belief, staying true to your dream and life all at the same time. That's probably why only a few actually get to truly live their dream. But no matter how much it scares you, if you truly believe you can accomplish it and you're prepared to put in the hours of work that it will take to get there, then you can. There is no hard, there is no easy. There is the goal, the price that must be paid and the eyes observing from a distance... Wondering...just maybe, if they could do the same. The Chip On My Shoulder I was lucky enough to have a great great man as a Grandfather. One with stories of adventures, daring and bravery. A lifetime of stories that showed a strength of character that you don't find. As my mum will know, his value was above rubies. Derrick Cooling - The Legend I wanted these kind of stories. I wanted to be able to sit my grandchildren down and be more than someone who coasts through life without making any ripples. I wanted to test myself, inspire people and push the boundaries and limits that were laid out by other men. Probably because I'm stubborn as you like but also because I can't let my life be defined by the opinion and outlook of others. It is this idea that pushes me to want it... I want it so bad it hurts and I'll take all of the pain that I need to take until I've done enough to get there. I suppose you can call that passion, some might call it stupidity but either way, I'll keep the pedals turning until I get there. I may find that my limits are the same or less than the boundaries set out by others... I just need to see it for myself. The question people always ask is "what will you do when you've done that?" like this pursuit of better is all about getting a medal or race finishers t-shirt. Really?! Consider for a moment that I don't climb onto this bike or slip into my running shoes because I want a mass produced medal or a cheap finishers t-shirt, I do those things that you might consider to be crazy because I love it. Belief Self belief is a very strange thing. It's a bit like being 'The One'. Nobody can tell how to, you just kind of know it. Deep deep down you know that there is something inside you that is worth pushing for. It all sounds a bit like Neo in the Matrix but it's pretty much the same. The difficult thing is that when you've got a bit of self belief and you're working on your dream, the noises of the doubters start to stir. A great many people will tell you that they don't think you can do that, or go that fast, or hold that power. You might not be able to but how do they know? These are the types of fear based boundaries and limits that people set and who will readily tell you about because maybe their insecurity wont let them believe that its possible. This is where you can get busy proving them wrong, or sometimes right (be prepared to eat some humble pie if you get it wrong). But just give it a go. Find out for yourself! One of my favourite quotes that I think embodies self belief; The general idea is, if you want to do something bigger, or go faster than anyone has ever gone before, then you're going to need to do things people have never done before. Be that training harder, hurting more, more hours training, something will need to be different for you to get a different result to everyone else... Unless you're incredibly lucky and genetically gifted that is! My one piece of advice is cut away the people who let fear guide them. No matter how hard you try, there will be times when your strength wavers and when you need people around you to remind you that you can do it. Remember, your vibe attracts your tribe. Be positive, believe in yourself and you will attract people who do the same. Iron Doesn't Break, It Bends If you want to do unreasonable things, you need to be an unreasonable person. Now life isn't black and white and it takes maturity to realise that (31 years old and I've only just sussed it out). A truer statement is something along the lines of; Be unreasonable in your aims but flexible in your approach . There is a reason the race is called an Ironman and not a Diamondman. Yes diamond is harder than Iron, but it's so hard it's brittle. Iron is malleable and can bend and change shape but remains strong. Life has a funny way of throwing a spanner into the intricate works of your best thought out plan. That is something that you need to prepare and account for. From an athlete's perspective this usually appears as some unforeseen engagement that you're obliged to attend, illness, injury or broken equipment. All of these things can stop you training and could leave you feeling like you're falling behind. You need to be honest with yourself about your program and what you can realistically fit around life. If you're constantly beating yourself up about not having time for that brick run or that lunch swim session then training will end up being a negative experience. Set achievable targets that really push you, set a realistic program that you can complete and little goals that you can tick off every week. Take that approach and you'll start giving yourself a regular pat on the back and start feeling good about it. The bottom line is that training is tough enough without giving yourself a hard time. That's the flexibility part. The unreasonable part comes sits the other side of the seesaw. Sometimes you're going to need to duck out of trips, social events or nights out if you want to put the time in. But then if you're truly passionate about what you're doing then this shouldn't bother you. You might need to get used to saying no to a lot of things so you can say one massive "YESSSSSSSSSS!!!" as you cross the finish line with a new PB. Follow the dream, take the hard route even though its painful. It will be worth it in the end. No Man Is An Island I've always considered myself a bit of a lone wolf type. I don't really fit well with a big group of friends and much prefer to walk my own path. At times this has been quite a lonely walk but a walk that I knew I could complete if I remained strong and true to myself. One thing I always remind myself of is the toughest climbs lead to the greatest destination. It's probably not that the place you get to is any better than another place, the beauty of the destination is defined by the pain you went through to get there. Something I have definitely realised is that behind any strong Ironman or Ironwoman is an incredible support network. There isn't really much to say about the support network because if you're reading this you probably already know how valuable these people are. My only advice is; Take the time to let them know that they are important to you and you value their contribution on your journey. Take the time to put special effort in with your partner who probably doesn't want to talk about your new aero wheels at dinner. Get a round in when people have come to watch you race, its a bloody long day for them and they probably need a drink to sooth the vocal cords that have been shouting your name for the last umpteen hours. Here are a few shout outs to my support crew, who have accompanied me on my journey so far and who I couldn't have done it without; Jo, my babe of a fiancée and the Chairwoman of my fan club. She needs a medal for the amount of times she has picked me up off the floor after I've overdosed on exercise. Thank you for supporting me at all of my races, keeping me fed and helping me keep my sh*t together. Definitely couldn't do it without you! Mum & Huw, for not only supporting me at my events, but covering every fence post, lamppost and tree on 'The Tumble' with motivational posters for my Everesting attempt, and half of the time participating in the events too! I think you've both probably loathed me at times thanks to some of the challenges I've laid down so you both get brownie points for sense of humour and cheerfulness in the face of adversity. Chief, for being my own personal Mr Motivator; always reminding me that there's something special inside and a reason to believe, giving me endless motivational quotes and for the hours upon hours of phone calls listening to me talking through training plans, equipment and race tactics. Think you could probably write a book with all the triathlon knowledge you've got! Sister, for believing in me, worrying I'm going to drop dead at a moments notice for pushing too hard and pestering Jo through every minute of every race. Can't forget Georgia aka Treasures... my own little race mascot! If after all that you're still struggling for motivation... have a watch of my favourite pre-race video. This should sort you out! ← Back to the blog Train with Horsepower If that is how you like your coaching, straight and built for your race, take a look at the training plans or see how coaching works . blog/f/the-lightest-disc-brake-bike/inde.body: Skip to content ☰ Home Coached by Tom Female Performance Plan Only Plan Store About Us Blog Contact Blog / 25 January 2021 The Lightest Disc Brake Bike??? By Tom Cooling · 25 January 2021 The Intro I've always been a bit of a weight weenie and have a massive love of riding up hill and have spent the last few years participating in the UK hill climb season. As many of you will know hill climbs on a bike are a brutal affair. It's basically a lung busting individual time trial up a nominated climb. It might be 1 minute or 15minutes but either way, you know you're going deep from the start. The hill climb scene isn't subject to the UCI minimum bike weight rules so a massive part of racing hill climbs and the scene in general is modifying your bike to be as light as is possible. This modifying used to be mainly drilling holes in stuff to remove material but now thanks to many manufacturers catering to this niche area, you can now adorn your bike with super light components to complement your handy Dremel work. Anyhow, in this blog I'm going to tell you about a bit of bike history that led to me building up what was at the time of writing, the lightest disc brake hill climb bike in the UK... or the world??? The Build Up... keep reading So over my hill climb years I've been through a few steeds in the quest of light. It all started when I bought my first proper bike, a Colnago Extreme C (C meaning Climber). A frame that was designed specifically for the 2004 Tour de France Alpe d'Huez time trial. A frame so good that many of the riders carried on riding it after the uphill race of truth. Now for me this bike was mega, traditional geometry which looks amazing, light (not by a hill climb standard) and stiff and just had composure and class for days. I Everested on it and even got to take it to the Alps to send it up Alpe d'Huez albeit with a broken rib. I should have never sold it but at 7.4kgs I needed something lighter. Then, after a brief foray with an S-Works Tarmac SL5 that I just didn't enjoy I found the razer blade of road bikes. Stiff as you like and light as a feather... Drum roll please! May I introduce the beautiful Canyon Ultimate CF SLX (2014). This was the kind of bike you ride and it just feels alive under you, like a really overly energetic Border Collie pup wanting to run everywhere, or smash it up every hill in sight in this case. The Canyon weighed in at a feathery 6.25kgs wearing my own hand-built Wheels by TC carbon wheels, Sram RED eTap groupset and carbon everything else. After 2 x haute routes in 2019 (Dolomites and Alps) where the Canyon didn't put a foot wrong, I set about turning it into a machine even more specialised at going up hill ready for the UK hill climb season. This involved stripping off the etap front mech, fitting a lighter stem and handlebars, a carbon version of my much loved SMP saddle and some pretty sexy EE Cycleworks brake calipers. All of these changes got me under the magic 6kg mark including pedals. Canyon V2... keep reading So after what felt like a pretty good hill climb season I wanted lighter. I'd seen bikes at the nationals under 5kgs... an entire kilogram lighter than mine... obviously that's why the likes of Dan Evan, Ed Laverack and Andrew Feather were dropping me like a bad habit??? A friend of mine had recently sent his bike off to Fat Creations, Alister and Beckie worked wonders on his and stripped off SO much weight losing the original paint job. I love a bit of DIY so I got in touch with Alister and he very kindly offered to guide me through the process and Beckie make up the stencils for my logo. Out came the razor blade, wet&dry and elbow grease...about a week or so later beauty emerged... 1kgs for the frame and fork! A bit of stenciling here and spraying there and pow... this was my finished design. I decided to swap out the electronic groupset in favour of the lighter and less problematic mechanical. The groupset was a mixture of Sram RED 10 speed and 11 speed parts paired with a 1x GARBARUK chainring and another pair of Wheels by TC lightweight clinchers. The outcome... 5.540kgs including pedals and a Wahoo mount. As with any project, when its complete sometimes you lose the love for it because its no longer a work in progress. This bike was awesome, an absolute missile on the hills but I had to let it go.... I had bigger ideas. The Big Idea - A Disc Brake Hill Climb Bike You'll notice almost any really serious hill climb bike uses rim brakes. It's because both the frames and components tend to be lighter lighter... but what if someone had a crack at a disc brake hill climb bike? I know it wouldn't get down to the same crazy light weights of some of the rim brakers, but my would it be cool and possibly faster in real world situations. I've got eyes on a strong performance in the Haute Route Dolomites 2021 and would love to have a crack at another everesting (but this time go fast) so I thought, disc brakes are the one. So to keep it realistic, I'd have to forget about the 5kg golden weight barrier for a rim brake hill climb bike and focus my sights in on 6kgs which seems to be the equivalent for a disc bike. The Base Bike I promptly stripped the bike of all the components it came with - wheels, Cannondale Hollowgram SI crank, seatpost, bottom bracket etc and began building a spec. The Rough Spec I knew it needed to run SRAM Red because that was the lightest but I didn't want electronic. I love the simplicity of a mechanical groupset and enjoy being able to remedy any issues that might arise myself. I've always loved the super light alloy SISL2 crankset so that had to go on. A silky smooth C-BEAR ceramic bottom bracket. Extralite Hyper Stems are hard to beat and look awesome. Lightweight carbon seatpost saved over 100grams on the stock carbon item. My carbon SMP saddle. Not the lightest at 130grams but my bum loves it. The Wheelset Which brings me neatly onto the wheels... now I've been building seriously for around 5 years and have already built some epic hoops but I wanted this set to be my finest.... boy were they that! Key requirements were: Obviously lightweight, but not at the expense of usability. They had to be tubeless ready clinchers because I need this bike to be completely useable and I want the self sufficiency clinchers bring even at the expense of a bit of weight. I wanted an easily serviceable hub that wasn't brittle so Extralite was out. I settled on a pair of beautiful Light Bicycle Falcon Pro AR35 rims laced to Carbon TI X-Hub SP Disc hubs with the all time favourite Sapim CX-RAY bladed spokes and SAPIM alloy nipples. If you fancy a wheelset like this or have a dream build in mind, get in touch with Wheels by TC . The Big Reveal - The 5.895gram Disc Brake Hill Climb Bike So its probably time to show the bike off a bit. I'm sorry to do this to Specialized after all of the hullabaloo they made about the new Aethos that weighs in at a portly 5.9kgs and costs a frankly crazy £11k, but here goes.... My sub 5.985gram Cannondale Supersix Evo Hi-Mod Disc So Whats Next? The bike is AMAZING to ride, rides as well as the Canyon but the difference in braking is next level as you'd expect. I've got some big and quite cool plans in the pipeline for this bike but they are more than deserving of another blog that will follow shortly. Not only will this bike be one of the lightest disc brake bikes out there, its soon to be potentially the only 1x12 speed mechanical disc brake bikes in the world.... yes I know SRAM don't make one... Thanks for reading. Any questions about the build or wheel building please get in touch. blog/f/tits-up---how-to-deal-with-failur.body: Skip to content ☰ Home Coached by Tom Female Performance Plan Only Plan Store About Us Blog Contact Blog / 25 January 2021 Tits Up - How to Deal with Failure By Tom Cooling · 25 January 2021 How to deal with failure... The story of the race that never was... So this year I had one aim... Get fit enough to finish in the top 10 at the Long Distance Alpe d'Huez Triathlon in July. Simple right?! Well last October I got busy with a training program that would turn me into a serious contender. For 9 months I plugged away through rain, cold, wind, fatigue and illness trying to beat out kind of average athlete and emerge a serious threat to the apple cart. My first race of the season was the DBMAX Brecon Titan Half plus Ironman in June. I was aiming to use this as a springboard to test my fitness and give me an idea of the power I could hold on the bike and still put together a good run. After leaving the water in 24th position I hit the bike course hard. I held a 300w normalised power on the 60 mile bike course and climbed to 3rd position whilst setting the fastest bike split of the day. I ended up finishing an overall 2nd with a 1 hr 31 minute run which was a great morale boost. After the race I went away for a much needed break to Menorca. Put in a good bit of swimming and a few runs in the heat but mainly used the time to recoup and have some quality time with my partner Jo. I came back 2kgs heavier despite watching my food intake. This sent me on a bit of a downward spiral as I'd always viewed my light weight and high power output as my key weapon. In panic I picked up the training and cut my calorie intake in an attempt to lose the weight. I started stressing about every little thing on the bike; how much it weighed, was there any marginal gain to be seen from changing to ceramic parts. In a word I was all over the place. The calm and quiet confidence that had seen me ok at the Brecon Titan was gone and replaced with an anxious fool who did a good job of boring the hell out of his partner by repeatedly talking through the intricacies of wheelset weight vs aerodynamic advantage and how that relationship was affected by gradient. After so much umming and arrring I relied on Best Bike Split for the correct bike and wheel combo. In retrospect I should have taken the TT bike despite the mega 12,000ft of climbing. The day before the race. Hopes were high! Quick bike check and warm up spin up the Alpe d'Huez climb complete Finally race day came around and I crossed my fingers and hoped the nerves would calm down and I could put in a performance that would do my big dream justice. I arrived down at T1 feeling nervous, it was a cold clear morning. The 12 mile descent from Huez to Lac du Verney sapped at the bodyheat, not something you want when you're about to swim in 15 degree water. My support crew appeared and I said my goodbyes and headed down to the lake entrance. My nerves turned to excitement as I jumped into the water, shortly followed by an "oh sh*t that's cold!" I'd been working really hard on my swimming and wanted to leave the water in the top 100 or so swimmers because I knew I had a strong bike and good run to make up the places. I made my way to where I imagined the centre of the pack would be hoping to catch some fast feet and draft my way around. As the other 1500+ competitors filed into the water the support boat pushed the front of the group back. This only served to cram us all tighter together. After about 10 minutes of pushing back and forth the gun went off and the melee began. I had swum all of 20 meters before being pushed under the water by two swimmers either side of me coming together. As I tried to relax and come up swimmers who were behind me came over the top... I started swallowing water panicking as I tried to come up to the surface. The water was a mix of foaming white water and wetsuit clad bodies, all thrashing to get clear of this icy cold hell hole. During what felt like a fight with the water and the other athletes I took one kick to the mouth and another to the left of my chest. I felt like I had an unbearably tight band around my torso as the waves of panic attack washed over me. Hyperventilating and feeling like I was being choked by my wetsuit I pulled it off my throat only for the freezing cold water to gush in and add to the suffering. I rolled onto my back and tried to calm myself before rolling back over to watch the front of the race disappear around the first buoy. The feeling of disappointment was as overwhelming as the clamp around my chest tightened. Not wanting to be a complete failure and let down to my family I started to try and swim again. I couldn't front crawl because every time my face entered the chest clamp stopped me breathing... Breaststroke was my only option. I pushed on and exited the lake in around 500th position and jumped onto the bike hoping the chest tightness would ease off. As the miles ticked by I knew something wasn't right. I couldn't breathe deeply, the tight band around my chest was ever present. I kept trying to focus on a good aero position on the bike and a smooth pedal stroke but every time I glanced down at my power meter I was putting out nearly 100w less than I had planned. I just couldn't make the bike move and every time I pushed a bit harder the chest band tightened. 70 miles in the alps is a long time to think about a broken dream. Watching people twice my weight sail past me on the climbs was absolutely heart breaking, especially after coming to the race with such high ambitions. The disappointment brought me to tears on so many times as the miles rolled painfully by. As usual I'd given Jo (my partner) an annotated map of where I'd be on the course at what time. When I was over 1 hour late at the top of the famous Alpe d'Huez climb she knew something was wrong as I'm usually bang on with my timings. Eventually I appeared, swerving from left to right grimacing as I looked down at the handlebars. She was waiting with my folks at our apartment that fronted onto the main climb. I had been praying for the last 3 hours that they would be there and had pitched my pain threshold to that point. I knew the race was over because I could barely cycle, let alone run. I climbed the 21 hairpin bends of Alpe d'Huez in tears with a stream of snot pouring from my nose. When I finally made it to Jo, I literally rode into her before collapsing onto the floor. The dream was over. Such a bad place... My folks drove me to the medical tent at the event village where the awesome medical staff examined me and confirmed I had two broken ribs... that was some consolation as it meant I'd not finished for a good reason. The DNF (did not finish) hit me so hard because I couldn't quite grasp that despite putting in all of the time training and having a bike that was literally built for that climb (Colnago Extreme C), something outside of my control would be able to derail my grand plan. Fixing broken ribs with beer... #science I think this race failure served a good lesson for many reasons, the main two were needing to be honest with myself about my swimming ability and where I should position myself in a mass swim start, and that I need to accept that there will sometimes be a bad day at the office. I also took a lot from the pre-race experience as a guide of what not to do. One of my favourite quotes I've now recovered from the ribs and have full mobility. I've been using the downtime to focus on my swim technique which has yielded huge efficiency savings in the water. The moral of the story is, triathlon is a game of luck. The sh*t days will come regardless of how hard you've trained. You just need to make it count when lady luck is smiling at you. This one is definitely dedicated to family. I was lucky enough that I couldn't sit and dwell about my DNF because I had a promise to keep. For the weeks and months leading up to the race I'd been trying to convince my partner and folks that they had to tackle the 21 hairpins at Alpe d'Huez. I just couldn't let them go there without doing it. So the day after the race I nailed 500mg of codeine and headed out to chaperone them up the mountain... a few hours, a coffee stop and an amazing burger at the 'O' bar in Huez, we finished a beautiful ride that really put a great end to the trip. Jo, Mum & Huw on the podium celebrating Me in pain standing next to my Mountain Goat ← Back to the blog Train with Horsepower If that is how you like your coaching, straight and built for your race, take a look at the training plans or see how coaching works . blog/f/train-easier-than-you-think/index.body: Skip to content ☰ Home Coached by Tom Female Performance Plan Only Plan Store About Us Blog Contact Blog / 4 August 2026 Why Most of Your Training Should Be Easier Than You Think By Tom Cooling · 4 August 2026 If I had to fix one thing about how most amateurs train, it'd be this: they ride their easy days too hard and their hard days too easy. The backbone of good endurance training is controlled aerobic work, done at an honest, repeatable intensity, most of the time. Intensity is the seasoning, not the meal. Why is everyone stuck in the grey zone? Because it feels productive. A steady effort that leaves you a bit cooked feels like work, so people default to it every session. The problem is that this middle ground, hard enough to pile up fatigue but not hard enough to force a proper adaptation, gives you the cost of hard training without the reward of it. You're tired all the time and improving slowly. I've coached plenty of people who were training their socks off in exactly this zone and getting nowhere, and the fix was to make them go easier, which they hated for about three weeks and then loved. Easy should be genuinely easy. Conversational, low heart rate, the sort of ride where you finish and think you barely did anything. That's the point. It builds the aerobic engine, the mitochondria, the fat metabolism, the capillary bed, without digging a hole. And when the hard day comes around, you're fresh enough to actually go hard. The physiology behind this isn't mysterious. Low-intensity aerobic work drives the adaptations that make you an endurance athlete: more and bigger mitochondria to produce energy aerobically, better fat oxidation so you spare your limited carbohydrate stores, and a denser capillary bed to deliver oxygen and clear waste. Crucially, these adaptations respond to volume, to time accumulated, and volume is only possible if the intensity is low enough that you can recover and come back and do it again tomorrow. Push the easy days into the grey zone and you can't accumulate the volume, because you're too tired, so you lose the exact adaptation the easy days exist to produce. You get less base off more suffering. That's the trap. What does the backbone look like? Most of the volume should be sub-threshold: aerobic and controlled, below the point where it starts to hurt in a way you have to fight. How I structure the year around that depends on how far out the race is. More than twelve weeks to the race: the emphasis is sub-threshold progressive overload. You build time-in-zone at tempo, sweet-spot and sub-threshold week on week, growing the durable aerobic base that everything else sits on. Patient, unglamorous, and the highest-return work there is at this range. Twelve weeks or less: the plan tips polarised, broadly seventy to eighty per cent easy and twenty to thirty per cent genuinely hard, with a growing sprinkle of race-intensity work as race day approaches. The hard days get sharper and more specific; the easy days stay honestly easy to pay for them. The through-line in both is the same. The bulk of your training is aerobic and controlled. What changes near the race is how the small hard slice gets spent. Why sub-threshold rather than just easy and hard? Because there's enormous value in the controlled work that sits just below your threshold, and it gets unfairly lumped in with the useless grey zone. There's a difference between drifting into no-man's-land on an easy day, which is a mistake, and deliberately doing a tempo, sweet-spot or sub-threshold session with a clear target and a clear purpose, which is not. The first is uncontrolled and leaves you tired for no gain. The second is one of the highest-return sessions in endurance training, especially when the race is a long way off. The reason it works is durability. Long-course racing isn't won by your one-minute power or even really by your threshold; it's won by how much of your ability you can still access after four, six, eight hours of work. Progressive sub-threshold volume, built patiently, is what raises that durable ceiling. It teaches the body to hold a strong aerobic effort for a long time without falling apart. Done properly, week on week, with the time-in-zone climbing gradually, it's the quiet backbone that everything specific gets bolted onto later. The trick is that it still has to be controlled. Sub-threshold means below threshold, on purpose, at a target, not "as hard as I can hold." The moment it creeps up into threshold and beyond on every session, you're back in the grey zone with extra steps. When does intensity actually earn its place? Intensity is a tool, and like any tool it's for a specific job. It earns its place when: You're inside the sharpening window and need to lift the top end for a specific event demand. You've got a limiter that only high-intensity work moves, like a weak VO2 ceiling for a punchy course. The session is properly dosed. A VO2 block with only a few minutes of actual work in it is a waste of a hard day. The sessions that build fitness carry real accumulated time at the target, with recoveries long enough to let you hit the next rep. Half-hearted intensity is the worst of both worlds. One more thing people miss: heat work is intense work. A heat-acclimation turbo session might read as soft wattage, but physiologically it lands in the hard budget. If you're running a heat block, your conventional intensity has to shrink to make room, or it's all hard, all the time, and you crack. Easy stays easy so the hard, in whatever form, can be hard. So how do I know if I'm doing it right? Ask two honest questions after each session. On an easy day: could I have held a conversation the whole time and finished feeling I could do it again tomorrow? If not, it wasn't easy. On a hard day: did I actually reach the intensity the session was built for, or did I fade into the grey zone halfway through? If you can't give the right answer to both, you're training in the middle, and the middle is where progress goes to stall. Get the easy days easy and the hard days hard. The aerobic backbone does the quiet, enormous work; intensity, used sparingly and dosed properly, puts the edge on top. That order matters, and most people have it backwards. ← Back to the blog Train with Horsepower If that is how you like your coaching, straight and built for your race, take a look at the training plans or see how coaching works . coached/index.html.body: Skip to content ☰ Home Coached by Tom Female Performance Plan Only Plan Store About Us Blog Contact Plan Only · £120 a month A plan I build for you, block by block The same coaching my fully coached athletes get, written for you, block by block, for £120 a month. I build your programme myself and give you honest feedback on every session you complete. The only difference is the contact: no calls, and I am not on call day to day. The coaching in the plan is exactly the same. Apply for Plan Only What you get for £120 a month A plan built for you, not pulled off a shelf. I write your programme myself, block by block, exactly the way I do for my fully coached athletes. At the end of each block I go through everything you've done, tell you straight what I see, and build the next block around where you actually are, not where some plan guessed you'd be. The only thing you don't get compared to full coaching is the contact. No catch-up calls, and I'm not on hand day to day. The coaching that goes into the plan itself is exactly the same: a real coach shaping your training around your life and your numbers, just without the premium of unlimited access. It starts with you A proper intake: your target event, your history, your week, your numbers and the hours you actually have. Your plan arrives block by block Built around your life and your event, three weeks at a time, so it stays current with how your training is actually going rather than a whole year written on day one. Feedback on every completed session I read the sessions you complete against what was asked, using your actual data, and tell you what it means and what happens next. A race plan before every start line Pacing, fuelling and strategy for your event, in your hands before you get there. A Horsepower athlete finishing Challenge Almere-Amsterdam Honest answers Is there a call every week? No. Plan Only is built around the work and the why, delivered in writing so you can go back to it. If you want calls, WhatsApp and race-day strategy built together, that is Coached by Tom. What if my numbers change or life gets in the way? The plan moves. When your data shifts or a week falls apart, the next block reflects it. That is the point of building it block by block instead of all at once. Which sports do you coach? Triathlon across every distance, road and ultra running, and cycling from sportives to ultra-distance. If you have a target event, I can build for it. Can I upgrade later? Yes. If you want me directly, you can move to Coached by Tom when a place is open. Where it differs from full coaching There are no scheduled calls and I am not on call day to day. What you get is a programme I build around your life and your event, with real feedback on the sessions you actually do. If you want me in your corner for all of it, look at Coached by Tom. Coached by Tom Ready to start? Tell me about your event and your season and I'll take it from there. Apply for Plan Only In their words What athletes say about Horsepower ★★★★★ 5 from 15 Google reviews ‹ Tom is a great coach and has helped massively with my cycling, helping me achieve results I wouldn't have thought possible previously. Ian C Cycling athlete I can't recommend Tom enough. Over the past year, the support, structure, and guidance I received helped me progress massively and achieve my Ironman goal, finishing in 11h13. jc b Ironman finisher, 11h13 I've been working with Tom at Horsepower Coaching for the past year, it was the best decision I made for my cycling and I cannot recommend Tom highly enough to anyone seeking a cycling coach. His personalised approach, attention to detail, and unwavering support have been amazing. What sets Tom apart is his genuine passion for both coaching and wanting you to succeed. His training is a great balance between professional and friendly, and is always able to adapt to anything and everything. He always takes the time to provide personalised regular and understandable feedback, being there to answer any questions no matter how small. Lastly the level of support he provided on the day of the event was amazing. If you're looking for a coach who will go the extra mile and genuinely care about your progress, Tom is the one to choose. Rebecca W Cycling athlete I've been working with Tom for over a year now, and after initially being apprehensive about investing in a coach, it's turned out to be a great decision, made all the better by how good of a coach Tom is. Having decided to train for another Ironman with ever increasing work and family commitments, it was important that my training sessions were efficient and high quality, and Tom has delivered this, and more. Tom is a wealth of knowledge, friendly, adaptable, patient with injuries, and a great mentor. Highly recommended. Guy L Ironman athlete Tom and I worked together for 2 seasons, covering sprint and middle distance triathlons and a road racing season. During that time, my running came on beyond my wildest expectations and I hit the start line on my first 70.3 fully prepared and in the best shape I've been in a while. His thorough and detailed approach gave my a tangible roadmap for the work ahead, and his open and friendly nature helped me engage with the process throughout. I would thoroughly recommend Tom as a coach, whatever your goal or current standard. Rob T Triathlon and road racing Tom has been an absolutely epic coach. His knowledge is mega and I've learnt so much through being coached by Horsepower. Impressively have podiumed at every Triathlon I've done since working with Tom and still seeing mega gains month on month. Get Bent Yoga Triathlete Tom has been a great coach, who has developed me towards being the best I can be at road cycling. A very friendly, but firm approach that gets the best out of you. I fully recommend Tom to anybody who would be interested in improving themselves as an athlete.
